scenarios.title: System Design: Clickstream Pipeline
scenarios.situation: Interview prompt: 'Design a pipeline for 100K events/sec clickstream: real-time dashboard (1-min latency) + ML training data (daily). Walk me through your design.'
scenarios.prompt: What structure makes this answer strong?
choices: Name-drop Kafka, Flink, and Spark and describe each

Structure by requirements then components: state the two latency tiers explicitly, then trace one event through the design (edge collection → durable log → stream processor for the 1-min aggregates → raw landing for the daily batch/ML), naming the trade-off at each choice (why a log not a queue, delivery semantics, backpressure handling, reprocessing story) — and state what you'd cut under time pressure
Draw a complex diagram with every tool you know
Say you'd use a managed service for everything
scenarios.why: System design interviews score decision-making, not tool recitation. The two-tier requirement IS the design driver — everything follows from it. Tracing one event proves you understand data flow, not just boxes. Naming trade-offs at each choice (with the alternative you rejected and why) is what distinguishes senior answers. The 'what I'd cut' shows prioritization under constraints — exactly what the job requires.
scenarios.hint: What are the two different things being asked for — and what does each one demand from the architecture?
objectives: Structure system design answers by requirements and trade-offs
evidence: Trace one event from browser to both consumers

scenarios.title: The Pipeline War Story
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'Tell me about a hard pipeline failure you debugged.' You have one: the silent 2%/week row drop from a validation rule change. Last time you told it, you rambled for 6 minutes on background.
scenarios.prompt: How do you structure the story?
choices: Tell it chronologically with all the technical detail — depth impresses

STAR with systems thinking: Situation (30s: the drift, the stakes), Task (your ownership), Action as a TRACE (symptom → hypothesis → evidence at each stage → the validation rule diff that proved it → the fix), Result quantified (2%/week stopped, reconciliation monitoring added). End with the structural lesson (silent drops need stage-count reconciliation). 3 minutes, then invite questions
Pick a simpler story that's easier to tell
Focus on the fix, skip the debugging process
scenarios.why: Behavioral-with-depth interviews test how you THINK under ambiguity, and the debugging trace IS the evidence: hypothesis → evidence → conclusion at each step shows systematic reasoning, not luck. The structural lesson ('what I changed so this class of failure can't recur') is what elevates it from anecdote to senior signal. 3 minutes respects their time; 'invite questions' lets them probe depth where they care.
scenarios.hint: What is the interviewer actually evaluating — the bug, or your path from symptom to proof?
objectives: Tell debugging stories as hypothesis-evidence traces
evidence: State the structural lesson from your war story in one sentence

scenarios.title: The Trade-off Question
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'Your pipeline needs exactly-once. Do you choose Kafka transactions + Flink checkpointing, or idempotent writes? Defend your choice.'
scenarios.prompt: How do you answer a forced trade-off?
choices: Pick one confidently and defend it absolutely
Say 'it depends' and stop there

Refuse the false binary: compare on the axes that matter (operational complexity, end-to-end scope, failure modes), state the conditions for each (transactions when the sink supports it and the team can operate it; idempotent writes when sinks are dumb or teams are small — and note they're often COMBINED), then commit to a recommendation for THEIR context with the rollback plan if wrong
List every exactly-once technique you know
scenarios.why: Trade-off questions test judgment under constraints, not trivia. The strong answer compares on decision axes, names the conditions favoring each (not just the technologies), acknowledges the common synthesis (idempotent sinks UNDER transactional coordination), and commits — 'it depends' without a recommendation is evasion. The rollback plan shows you design for being wrong, which is senior-level thinking.
scenarios.hint: What would make you choose differently — team size, sink capabilities, or something else?
evidence: Name the condition that flips your recommendation

scenarios.title: Behavioral With Technical Depth
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'Tell me about a disagreement with a stakeholder over data.' You once fought the VP of Sales over the churn methodology (he wanted enterprise excluded). You caved at the time and now regret it.
scenarios.prompt: How do you tell this story honestly without looking weak?
choices: Invent a story where you won the argument
Blame the VP for being unreasonable

Tell it straight with the lesson: describe the pressure, what you did (caved), the consequence (the metric lost credibility when the exclusion leaked), and what you do NOW (the second-view compromise + methodology hold). Interviewers trust growth narratives over victory narratives — the lesson demonstrates the senior behavior better than a fake win
Say you've never had a disagreement
scenarios.why: Fabricated wins collapse under follow-up questions ('what exactly did you say?'). The growth narrative is stronger: it shows self-awareness, names the real consequence (credibility loss — interviewers know this failure mode), and demonstrates the CURRENT behavior pattern. 'What I do now' is the actual answer to 'how do you handle stakeholder pressure' — the story is just the vehicle.
scenarios.hint: Which is more credible under probing follow-ups — a perfect record, or a real lesson?
objectives: Tell growth narratives for behavioral questions
evidence: State your current stakeholder-pressure playbook in two sentences

scenarios.title: Take-Home Review: The Pipeline Design Doc
scenarios.situation: Your take-home was a pipeline design doc. In the review, the interviewer says: 'You chose batch for the fraud alerts. Our fraud team needs sub-minute. Walk me through your thinking.' Your doc actually says 'near-real-time micro-batch' — they skimmed it.
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle the misread?
choices: Correct them sharply — they should have read it

Assume good intent, bridge gracefully: 'Good catch to probe — the doc proposes micro-batch at 1-minute intervals, which hits sub-minute for the alert path; here's why I didn't go full streaming (the team's operational maturity, the reprocessing story for the model features)...' — then invite the deeper trade-off discussion. Never litigate the misread; use it as a springboard to show the reasoning
Agree batch was wrong and redesign on the spot
Stay silent and let them finish
scenarios.why: Correcting the interviewer creates an adversarial dynamic over a skim — you'll win the point and lose the interview. The bridge ('here's why I chose this') redirects to your reasoning, which is what's being evaluated. Naming the REAL trade-offs (operational maturity, reprocessing) shows the choice was deliberate, not default. Take-home reviews test how you defend decisions under pressure, not whether the doc was read.
scenarios.hint: What is being tested — your doc's wording, or your ability to defend the decision live?
objectives: Defend design decisions under misreading without defensiveness
evidence: State your micro-batch vs streaming trade-off in two sentences

scenarios.title: The On-Call Question
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'It's 3 AM, the pipeline is down, the dashboard is red, and you're on call. Walk me through your first 15 minutes.'
scenarios.prompt: What do they want to hear?
choices: That you'd fix it fast — speed is what matters at 3 AM
That you'd call the senior engineer immediately
Detailed debugging commands for their specific stack

The incident discipline: assess blast radius first (who's affected, is data wrong or just late?), communicate status early (a 5-minute 'I'm investigating, ETA update in 15' beats silence), follow the runbook before improvising, know when to escalate vs when to keep digging, and NEVER deploy an untested fix at 3 AM — stabilize (rerun from checkpoint, fail over) then root-cause in daylight
scenarios.why: The 3 AM question tests incident discipline, not heroics: blast-radius assessment prevents fixing the wrong thing; early communication prevents the stakeholder spiral; runbook-first prevents 3 AM improvisation disasters; the stabilize-now/root-cause-later split is the core on-call judgment. 'Fix it fast' signals cowboy tendencies; immediate escalation signals you can't own incidents. They want a calm operator.
scenarios.hint: What is the most dangerous thing you can do at 3 AM — and what should you do instead?
evidence: State your first three actions in order

scenarios.title: Whiteboard: Model the Domain
scenarios.situation: Whiteboard prompt: 'Model ride-sharing trip data for analytics: trips, drivers, riders, fares, surge pricing. 10 minutes.' The interviewer watches your first 60 seconds closely.
scenarios.prompt: How do you open?
choices: Start drawing tables immediately — speed shows confidence
Draw a perfect star schema from memory

Spend the first 2 minutes on questions and grain: 'What's the analytical question — per-trip economics or driver earnings? Is a trip one row, or do we need status-change history? How is surge stored — multiplier at trip time?' Then draw the grain decision first (trip-level fact, SCD2 driver dimension for rating/vehicle changes), narrating each choice. Questions-first beats tables-first
Ask for the ER diagram of the source system
scenarios.why: The first 60 seconds reveal whether you model the QUESTION or just the entities. Grain questions ('one row per what?') determine everything downstream — a trip fact vs a trip-status fact are different designs. Surge-as-fact-attribute vs dimension is a real decision. Narrating choices as you draw lets them follow your reasoning; silent perfect diagrams could be memorized. Whiteboard modeling is scored on the questions you ask.
scenarios.hint: What single decision determines the shape of everything else you'll draw?
objectives: Open modeling whiteboards with grain and question scoping
evidence: List your three opening questions for this domain

scenarios.title: The Failure Resume
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'What's the biggest mistake you've made as a data engineer?' You once dropped a production partition with a bad DELETE (no backup, 4 hours to recover from source). It's your best story and your scariest.
scenarios.prompt: How do you tell the DELETE story?
choices: Downplay it — pick a smaller mistake to seem safer
Blame the lack of guardrails at the company

Tell it fully: the mistake (unqualified DELETE on prod), the impact (4h recovery), the immediate response (owned it, recovered from source, communicated), and the structural changes (every destructive op now requires: dry-run SELECT first, partition-qualified predicates, backups before deletes, and prod write access reviewed). The story's value is the SYSTEM it produced — senior engineers are measured by what their mistakes built
Say you've never made a big mistake
scenarios.why: Every senior has a DELETE story; claiming otherwise destroys credibility. The interviewer wants the arc: mistake → ownership → systemic fix. The four structural changes are the real answer — they prove the mistake compounded into engineering judgment. 'Never made one' reads as junior or dishonest; blame reads as unaccountable. Own it, price it, show what it built.
scenarios.hint: What did the mistake BUILD — and is that worth more than the 4 hours it cost?
objectives: Tell failure stories as system-building narratives
evidence: List your destructive-operation checklist

domains.name: Spark & Distributed Processing
domains.description: Think in partitions: how distributed engines split work, shuffle data, and why skew kills performance.

scenarios.title: The Join That Never Finishes
scenarios.situation: A Spark job joining events (8B rows) to users (50M rows) has run 6 hours; one task shows 95% of the shuffle data. The cluster is otherwise idle.
scenarios.prompt: Diagnose and fix.
choices: Add more executors — the job needs more parallelism

Data skew on the join key: one or few keys hold most rows. Confirm via skewed-task metrics, then salt the heavy keys (or broadcast if the small side qualifies) — the fix is redistribution, not more hardware
Increase shuffle partitions to 10000 — more partitions always helps
Cache the users table — caching fixes slow joins
scenarios.why: One task with 95% of shuffle data is the textbook skew signature: more executors just add idle workers. The fix redistributes the hot keys (salting: split heavy keys across buckets, join, then re-aggregate) or avoids the shuffle (broadcast join if users table is small enough). Repartitioning without addressing key distribution just moves the skew. Caching helps repeated reads, not a skewed shuffle.
scenarios.hint: One task is drowning while others idle. Is that a resource problem or a distribution problem?
evidence: Stage UI
1 task: 480GB shuffle read; 199 tasks: <1GB each. Duration 6h+.
Key profile
Top 10 user_ids account for 61% of events.

scenarios.title: API Choice: DataFrame vs RDD vs SQL
scenarios.situation: Your team writes Spark jobs three ways: raw RDDs ('for control'), DataFrames, and Spark SQL strings. A new job needs to join 2TB of events with a 50GB dimension table, aggregate, and write partitioned output. The RDD advocate says DataFrames 'hide what's happening'.
scenarios.prompt: Which API do you choose, and why?
choices: RDDs — explicit control beats hidden optimization

DataFrames (or SQL): Catalyst optimizes the logical plan (predicate pushdown, join reordering, whole-stage codegen) in ways hand-written RDD code never will; the 2TB/50GB join gets broadcast-hash join automatically via AQE. RDDs are for when you need custom partitioning or low-level control — this job needs neither. 'Hiding' the optimization is the point
Spark SQL strings — they're the most readable
Mix all three in one job for flexibility
scenarios.why: The DataFrame API isn't hiding execution — it's exposing it to an optimizer that outperforms hand-tuned RDD code (whole-stage codegen alone is often 2-10x). For standard relational work (joins, aggregations), RDDs mean hand-rolling what Catalyst does provably better. The RDD advocate's 'control' is real but mispriced here: control over partitioning matters for iterative algorithms, not for a join-aggregate-write job.
scenarios.hint: What does the optimizer know about your join that your hand-written RDD code doesn't?
objectives: Choose DataFrame/SQL APIs for relational work; reserve RDDs for custom control
evidence: Name two Catalyst optimizations that apply to this join

scenarios.title: Partitioning: The 2TB Join
scenarios.situation: Your 2TB events ↔ 50GB dimension join runs 3 hours with 200 partitions. The Spark UI shows 190 tasks finishing in 2 minutes and 10 tasks running 2.5 hours. The dimension has a few mega-customers with millions of events each.
scenarios.prompt: What is the diagnosis and fix?
choices: Increase to 2000 partitions so the work spreads thinner
The cluster is too small; add executors

Skew: the 10 long tasks hold the mega-customer keys — more partitions won't help because the skewed KEYS still land together. Fix: salt the skewed keys (append random suffix, join on salted key, then aggregate the salt away) or isolate-and-broadcast the hot keys. Diagnose via the task duration distribution: a few tasks dominating = skew, not parallelism
Cache the dimension table first
scenarios.why: The task-duration distribution IS the diagnosis: 190 fast + 10 marathon = skew, full stop. More partitions subdivide the small keys further while the mega-keys still hash together — partition count can't fix key skew. Salting breaks the hot keys apart (at the cost of a two-phase join); hot-key isolation handles the few offenders specially. Executor count is irrelevant when 10 tasks hold all the work.
scenarios.hint: If 10 tasks take 2.5 hours and 190 take 2 minutes, what do the 10 have in common?
objectives: Diagnose skew from task distributions; apply salting
evidence: Explain why more partitions can't fix key skew

scenarios.title: Shuffle Diagnosis
scenarios.situation: Your job's Spark UI shows: 80% of time in 'shuffle read', spill to disk on every stage, and GC pauses. It does 5 consecutive groupBys on different keys over the same 500GB dataset.
scenarios.prompt: What is the structural fix?
choices: Increase executor memory to stop the spill
Use fewer, larger executors

Eliminate the redundant shuffles: each groupBy on a different key reshuffles 500GB — 5 shuffles = 2.5TB moved. Restructure to compute all aggregations in fewer passes (single pass with multiple aggregations where keys align, or repartition once to a common key), and persist the dataset if it's reused. Memory treats the spill symptom; shuffle count is the disease
Switch to RDDs for manual shuffle control
scenarios.why: Shuffle is the most expensive operation in Spark (network + disk + sort), and 5 different-key groupBys = 5 full reshuffles of 500GB. The spill and GC are downstream of moving 2.5TB unnecessarily. Restructuring the computation (combine aggregations, align keys, one repartition) attacks the 2.5TB directly; more memory just spills slightly later. Always count shuffles first — it's the first number in any Spark performance review.
scenarios.hint: How many times does the 500GB dataset cross the network — and how many of those crossings are necessary?
objectives: Minimize shuffle count as the primary Spark optimization
evidence: Compute the total shuffle volume: 5 groupBys × 500GB

scenarios.title: UDF vs Native
scenarios.situation: Your job uses a Python UDF to parse a custom timestamp format on 1TB of data. It runs 4 hours. A colleague rewrote it with native functions (to_timestamp with a format string) and it runs 25 minutes. The team still prefers UDFs because 'Python is more expressive'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the principled rule for UDF vs native?
choices: Always use UDFs — expressiveness beats speed
Rewrite all UDFs in Scala instead

Native first, UDF by exception: Python UDFs serialize every row out of the JVM (and pre-Arrow, row-at-a-time), killing whole-stage codegen — that's the 4h vs 25min. The rule: if native functions express it, use them; UDFs only for logic truly inexpressible natively (complex parsing, ML inference), and then prefer Pandas UDFs (vectorized) over row UDFs. 'Expressive' code that runs 10x slower is a liability at 1TB
It's fine — 4 hours is acceptable for a daily job
scenarios.why: The 10x gap has a physical cause: row UDFs force JVM↔Python serialization per row and disable whole-stage codegen (the JIT-compiled fast path). Native functions stay in the optimized pipeline. Pandas UDFs (Arrow vectorization) close most of the gap when UDFs are truly needed. The decision rule is economic: expressiveness is free at small scale and costs 10x at 1TB — choose by scale, not habit.
scenarios.hint: What happens to each row at the JVM/Python boundary — and what optimization dies because of it?
objectives: Apply the native-first rule; use vectorized UDFs by exception
evidence: Name the two costs of a row-based Python UDF

scenarios.title: Caching Strategy
scenarios.situation: Your job reads a 200GB dimension table, joins it 4 times in different branches, and writes 4 outputs. Someone added .cache() on the dimension 'for speed'. The job now OOMs — 200GB doesn't fit in the executors' memory.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct caching decision?
choices: Don't cache blindly: 4 reuses of 200GB MIGHT justify caching, but only if memory actually fits — otherwise the cache thrash (evict/recompute) is worse than recompute. Options: persist at a cheaper level only if it fits, reduce to the needed columns before caching (200GB → 20GB of used columns changes everything), or accept recompute if the read is cheap (columnar formats re-read fast). Cache is a bet that reuse-value exceeds memory-cost — do the arithmetic
Cache with DISK_ONLY so it never OOMs
Add more memory until the cache fits
Cache everything — memory is there to be used
scenarios.why: Cache is not free: it consumes memory that could serve execution, and a 200GB cache on smaller executors thrashes (constant evict/recompute = slower than no cache). The column-pruning insight is the real fix — joins usually need 5 of 50 columns, so project first and the cache becomes 20GB. The decision is arithmetic: (recompute cost × reuses) vs (memory cost + cache overhead). 'Cache for speed' without the math is how jobs OOM.
scenarios.hint: How many of the dimension's columns do the joins actually use — and what does the cache cost in evicted execution memory?
objectives: Make caching decisions with reuse-vs-memory arithmetic
evidence: State the caching decision formula

scenarios.title: Job Tuning: The Whole Picture
scenarios.situation: A critical job's runtime crept from 40 min to 3 hours over 6 months. Data grew 2x. The team wants to 'tune Spark configs' (memory, cores, shuffle partitions). The Spark UI shows: 1 massive stage (2.5h), skewed tasks, and spill.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct tuning order?
choices: Tune configs first — that's what 'Spark tuning' means

Fix the query before the configs: the 2.5h skewed stage with spill is a DATA problem (skew + shuffle volume), not a config problem. Order: (1) fix skew/salting, (2) reduce shuffle count, (3) prune columns/partition the read, (4) THEN set shuffle partitions ≈ 2-3x cores and size memory. Config tuning on a skewed 2.5h stage just makes the skew run on nicer hardware
Double the cluster size
Rewrite the job in a different engine
scenarios.why: Config tuning is the last 20%, not the first: no memory setting fixes key skew (the 10 marathon tasks still hold the hot keys), and no core count reduces a 2.5TB shuffle to less. The tuning order follows the cost stack — data shape (skew), operation count (shuffles), I/O (pruning), then configs. Teams that start with configs spend weeks for 10% gains; teams that fix the query get 5x in a day.
scenarios.hint: What would the perfect config change about the 10 tasks holding all the skewed keys?
objectives: Apply the query-first, configs-last tuning order
evidence: List the four tuning steps in order

scenarios.title: Broadcast Join Decision
scenarios.situation: Your job joins a 3TB fact table with a dimension table that was 8GB last quarter and is now 12GB. The join suddenly got 5x slower. spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold is at the default 10MB... but the join USED to broadcast fine via a hint.
scenarios.prompt: What happened, and what's the fix?
choices: The hint stopped working; remove it and let the optimizer decide
Increase the broadcast threshold to 20GB
The fact table is the problem; repartition it

The dimension outgrew the broadcast: at 12GB it exceeds executor memory for broadcast (the hint forces a broadcast that now OOMs/retries, or AQE disabled it). Fix: check the ACTUAL size (it may be 12GB with unused columns — prune to the 2GB actually joined), and only then decide: pruned-broadcast if it fits comfortably in memory, else sort-merge with proper partitioning. Broadcast is a memory bet — re-verify the bet when sizes change
scenarios.why: Broadcast joins copy the small table to EVERY executor — 12GB × 100 executors = 1.2TB of memory pressure, and the forced hint turns a graceful fallback into OOM/retry storms. The first move is always pruning: dimension tables carry dozens of unused columns, and the joined 2GB often broadcasts fine. Threshold-raising without pruning just moves the OOM. Sizes drift; broadcast decisions must be re-verified, not set-and-forget.
scenarios.hint: What does a broadcast join copy, to where, and how many times?
objectives: Re-verify broadcast decisions as table sizes drift
evidence: Compute the cluster-wide memory cost of broadcasting 12GB to 100 executors

domains.name: CDC & Real-Time Patterns
domains.description: Change data capture, exactly-once semantics, and the streaming patterns behind real-time products.

scenarios.title: The Late Events That Broke the Dashboard
scenarios.situation: The real-time revenue dashboard dropped 12% at midnight, then 'recovered' at 2 AM. The streaming job uses event-time windows with a 1-hour watermark. Mobile events arrive up to 3 hours late.
scenarios.prompt: What happened and what is the correct design change?
choices: The job crashed at midnight — add alerting and restart it

Watermark too aggressive: 1-hour watermark drops events later than 1 hour as 'too late'. Mobile events (up to 3h late) were discarded, then a backfill/replay restored them. Fix: extend watermark per business tolerance, add a side output for late events, and monitor the late-event rate as a first-class metric
Increase the window size from 5 minutes to 1 hour
Switch from event time to processing time
scenarios.why: The midnight 'drop' was the watermark discarding late mobile events; the 2 AM 'recovery' was a replay/backfill re-adding them. Watermarks are a business decision disguised as config: how late is still useful? The durable design extends the watermark to cover the known lateness distribution, routes stragglers to a side output (counted, visible, correctable), and alerts on the late rate — because lateness WILL drift.
scenarios.hint: Events arrived; the system chose to ignore them. What made that choice, and was it the right threshold?
evidence: Dashboard
Revenue -12% 00:00–02:00, recovered after replay.
Job config
Event-time windows, watermark = 1h. Mobile p99 lateness = 2h47m.

scenarios.title: The Field That Renamed Itself
scenarios.situation: Upstream renamed `user_id` to `userId` in the events topic. The streaming job now writes nulls for the join key; downstream dashboards show 'unknown user' climbing. Nothing crashed — silent corruption.
scenarios.prompt: What is the systemic fix?
choices: Update the job to read `userId` and redeploy — quick fix

Schema registry with compatibility checks (BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE) in CI: breaking changes fail the producer's build before deploy. Plus: contract tests, a schema-change notification process, and downstream null-rate alerting to catch what slips through
Add a COALESCE(userId, user_id) to handle both names forever
Pin the consumer to the old topic version
scenarios.why: The rename is a symptom; the disease is ungoverned schema evolution. Renaming a field is a breaking change — a registry with compatibility enforcement would have failed the producer's CI before deploy. COALESCE is duct tape that accumulates. The durable system: registry + compatibility rules + producer-side contract tests + consumer null-rate alerts as the safety net. Silent nulls are the most expensive failure mode because they corrupt decisions, not just dashboards.
scenarios.hint: Why did nothing crash? What would have caught this before production?
evidence: Topic schema
v14: user_id (int) → v15: userId (string). No registry; producers deploy freely.
Downstream
'unknown user' share: 2% → 38% over 6 hours. No alerts fired.

scenarios.title: Delivery Semantics
scenarios.situation: Your CDC pipeline must keep the warehouse replica within 5 minutes of the source DB. The team debates: at-least-once + idempotent merges vs exactly-once transactions. The sink is a cloud warehouse with MERGE support.
scenarios.prompt: Which semantics do you choose?
choices: Exactly-once transactions end to end — it's the only correct choice
At-most-once — duplicates are worse than loss
It doesn't matter; the warehouse dedupes automatically

At-least-once delivery with idempotent MERGE on the primary key: duplicates collapse (same key → same row), ordering handled by the CDC timestamp (last-write-wins on event time), and the operational cost is far lower than distributed transactions. True exactly-once needs transactional sinks and adds coordination overhead — choose it only when the sink supports it cheaply AND duplicates are semantically dangerous (e.g., non-idempotent side effects)
scenarios.why: For CDC-to-warehouse, at-least-once + idempotent merge IS effectively-once for row state: the merge key makes redelivery a no-op, and event-time ordering resolves conflicts. Distributed exactly-once (Kafka transactions + transactional sink) buys little here while adding real operational complexity. The semantics choice follows the sink: idempotent sinks make at-least-once sufficient; non-idempotent side effects (emails, charges) are where exactly-once earns its cost.
scenarios.hint: What does a duplicate delivery DO to a MERGE on primary key — and what would it do to a 'send email' action?
objectives: Choose delivery semantics by sink idempotency
evidence: State the condition where exactly-once is worth its cost

scenarios.title: Schema Evolution
scenarios.situation: The source team adds a column to the orders table. Your CDC pipeline breaks: the warehouse MERGE fails on schema mismatch, and the Kafka consumer deserializes with the old Avro schema. This is the third breakage this quarter.
scenarios.prompt: What is the structural fix?
choices: Get the source team to stop changing the schema
Pin the source table schema and reject all changes

Build evolution-tolerant CDC: schema registry with BACKWARD compatibility checks in the producer's CI (additive changes only, no renames/retypes without versioning), consumers using schema resolution (read with writer's schema), and the warehouse merge tolerating new nullable columns (or an explicit schema-migration step in the pipeline). Additive-column breaks are a solved problem — the pipeline just wasn't built for evolution
Manually fix the pipeline each time — it's only quarterly
scenarios.why: Schema change is constant; breakage is a design choice. BACKWARD compatibility mode means new schemas can read old data (additive columns with defaults) — enforced in CI so breaking changes never ship. Schema resolution lets consumers handle both versions during rollout. The warehouse side needs an explicit policy (auto-add nullable columns vs gated migration), not a surprise MERGE failure. Quarterly manual fixes are a tax you'll pay forever.
scenarios.hint: Which direction of compatibility lets old consumers read new data — and where should it be enforced?
objectives: Design evolution-tolerant CDC with schema registry governance
evidence: Name the compatibility mode and where it's enforced

scenarios.title: Late Data Policy
scenarios.situation: Your streaming aggregations (hourly revenue) use event time with a 10-minute watermark. About 2% of events arrive later than 10 minutes (mobile offline mode). Those events are silently dropped from the hourly totals, and finance's numbers never reconcile.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct late-data policy?
choices: Extend the watermark to 2 hours so no data is late

Two-tier policy: keep the 10-minute watermark for the real-time view (fast, approximate), and run a periodic batch reconciliation (hourly/daily) that recomputes from the raw log INCLUDING late events, overwriting the streaming aggregates. The streaming layer optimizes for latency, the batch layer for correctness — the Lambda/Kappa reconciliation pattern. Silent dropping is never acceptable for money metrics
Drop late data — 2% is within tolerance
Use processing time so nothing is ever 'late'
scenarios.why: The watermark is a latency/correctness trade-off, not a data-deletion policy: 10 minutes gives fast results, 2 hours makes every dashboard 2 hours stale. The reconciliation tier resolves it — streaming for speed, batch for truth, with the batch overwriting. Finance reconciles against the batch-corrected numbers. 'Within tolerance' for money metrics is how you lose the finance team's trust permanently.
scenarios.hint: What is the watermark actually trading off — and which tier should finance read?
objectives: Design two-tier late-data policies: streaming + batch reconciliation
evidence: State which tier serves the real-time dashboard vs finance

scenarios.title: State Management
scenarios.situation: Your Flink job keeps 30 days of per-user session state. State size hit 800GB, checkpoints take 20 minutes, and recovery from a failure takes 45 minutes. The job is falling behind its SLA.
scenarios.prompt: How do you fix the state problem?
choices: Give the job more memory and faster disks for checkpoints

Attack state size structurally: set TTLs matching the business need (do sessions really need 30 days, or 7?), use incremental checkpoints (only changed state), consider state schema slimming (store aggregates, not raw events), and for very large state, evaluate whether the use case fits streaming at all (some session analytics belong in batch). 800GB of state is a design smell, not a hardware problem
It's fine — 45-minute recovery is acceptable
Split the job into 4 smaller jobs
scenarios.why: State size drives checkpoint time, recovery time, and memory pressure together — 800GB is the root of all three symptoms. TTLs aligned to actual business need (session timeout is usually hours/days, not 30) can cut state 5-10x. Incremental checkpoints only ship deltas. The deeper question is architectural honesty: 30-day session state in a stream processor is often batch work wearing a streaming costume. Hardware treats symptoms; state design cures.
scenarios.hint: What business question requires 30 days of per-user session state IN the stream processor?
objectives: Manage streaming state: TTLs, incremental checkpoints, fit assessment
evidence: Name three levers that reduce state size

scenarios.title: Exactly-Once Design
scenarios.situation: The new pipeline triggers customer emails from order events (shipment notifications). Duplicates mean double emails — a customer-facing bug. The team proposes Kafka transactions + exactly-once Flink + a transactional email API.
scenarios.prompt: Is this the right design?
choices: Yes — exactly-once everywhere is the safe choice
At-least-once is fine — customers don't mind double emails
Don't send emails from a streaming pipeline

Decompose the problem: exactly-once DELIVERY is impossible to guarantee to a non-transactional email API — so design for effectively-once EFFECTS instead: idempotency keys on the email send (same order → same email ID, provider dedupes), transactional producer for the Kafka side, and a reconciliation job that catches anything missed. The 'exactly-once everywhere' design is expensive AND still can't cover the email API's non-transactionality
scenarios.why: End-to-end exactly-once requires EVERY participant to be transactional — the email API isn't, so the chain has a non-transactional link and the guarantee is void regardless of Kafka/Flink settings. Idempotency keys move the guarantee to where it can actually hold: the effect (one email per order) rather than the delivery. This is the general principle: design idempotent effects, don't chase impossible delivery guarantees across system boundaries.
scenarios.hint: Which participant in this chain can NOT participate in a distributed transaction?
objectives: Design effectively-once effects with idempotency keys
evidence: Explain why the email API breaks the exactly-once chain

scenarios.title: Consumer Lag and Backfill
scenarios.situation: A downstream consumer was down for 6 hours; it now has 50M messages of lag. If it consumes at max speed, it'll take 10 hours to catch up — and its writes will hammer the warehouse during business hours. The topic retention is 7 days.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct recovery procedure?
choices: Controlled catch-up: rate-limit the consumer (or schedule heavy catch-up off-hours), consider a parallel batch backfill for the lag window (read the 6h from the topic/retention into a batch job, then resume streaming from the backfill point), and monitor warehouse load during recovery. Uncontrolled catch-up trades a 6h outage for a warehouse brownout affecting everyone
Let it consume as fast as possible — catch up ASAP
Skip the 50M messages — they're stale
Increase retention to 30 days first
scenarios.why: Recovery has its own blast radius: max-speed catch-up converts one consumer's outage into everyone's warehouse slowdown. The batch-backfill hybrid is the pro move — bulk-load the 6h window efficiently (batch is better at bulk than streaming), then resume the stream at the boundary. Rate-limiting/off-hours scheduling contains the impact. Retention only matters if the lag exceeds it — 6h vs 7 days is safe.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the warehouse when one consumer suddenly writes 10 hours of backlog at full speed?
objectives: Execute controlled consumer-lag recovery with batch hybrid
evidence: State when the batch-backfill hybrid beats pure catch-up

domains.name: Cost & Performance Tuning
domains.description: Make pipelines fast AND cheap: partitioning, file sizing, and the cost levers of modern data platforms.

scenarios.title: The $40k Monthly Query
scenarios.situation: The BigQuery bill tripled to $40k/month. One dashboard refresh scans 4TB; it runs 200x/day. The table is partitioned by ingestion time but queries filter by event date.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix, in priority order?
choices: Buy more BigQuery slots — the dashboard needs the capacity
Partition (or cluster) by the actual filter column (event date), add an aggregated mart for the dashboard's grain, cache results — attack the 4TB scan first: 200 × 4TB is the entire bill
Reduce dashboard refresh frequency to hourly
Move to a cheaper warehouse
scenarios.why: The partition column does not match the filter column, so every query scans everything: 200 × 4TB = 800TB scanned daily. Priority 1: repartition/cluster by event_date (prunes ~99% per query). Priority 2: pre-aggregate to the dashboard's grain (a 4TB scan becomes a 4GB scan). Priority 3: cache/schedule. Slot purchases and warehouse moves treat the symptom; the scan volume IS the disease. Measure bytes-scanned per query before and after — that metric is the bill.
scenarios.hint: What does the query filter on vs what the table is partitioned on? Multiply the mismatch by 200/day.
evidence: Billing
$40k/mo, top query: dashboard refresh, 4TB scanned, 200 runs/day.
Schema
Partitioned by _ingestion_time; queries filter on event_date.

scenarios.title: Right-Sizing the Cluster
scenarios.situation: Your Spark cluster runs 24/7 with 50 nodes. Utilization logs show: nights/weekends at 5%, business hours spiking to 80% for 3 hours, average 25%. The bill is $40K/month. Finance asks 'why does this cost so much?'
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct right-sizing strategy?
choices: Cut to 20 nodes — average utilization is only 25%
It's fine — $40K is normal for data platforms

Match capacity to the load curve: autoscaling (or scheduled scaling) for the baseline + burst, separate the 3-hour spike workloads onto ephemeral/burst capacity (spot/preemptible where retry-safe), and question the 24/7 baseline (can dev/test sleep nights/weekends?). Cutting to average guarantees the spike fails; the goal is paying for the curve, not the peak or the average
Move everything to spot instances
scenarios.why: Static clusters charge peak capacity 24/7: the 5%-utilization nights are pure waste, and cutting to the average breaks the spike. The load curve IS the sizing spec — autoscaling follows it, burst capacity (spot) handles the spike cheaply, and sleep schedules kill the idle baseline. 'Average utilization' is the wrong number; the integral under the curve vs the rectangle of static provisioning is the savings.
scenarios.hint: What are you paying for at 3 AM on Sunday — and what work is happening then?
objectives: Right-size with autoscaling, burst capacity, and sleep schedules
evidence: Name the three capacity tiers in the strategy

scenarios.title: Cutting the Scan Bill
scenarios.situation: Your cloud warehouse bill jumped 3x to $90K/month. The query history shows: full-table scans on the 50TB events table by 30 analysts, no partition pruning (queries filter on non-partition columns), and the same daily aggregations recomputed by 12 different dbt models.
scenarios.prompt: What is the systematic fix?
choices: Negotiate a discount with the vendor
Tell analysts to query less

Attack the scan volume structurally: partition/cluster the events table on the actual filter columns (event_date), build ONE shared daily aggregate mart that the 12 models read instead of recomputing, set up query monitoring with per-team cost attribution, and add guardrails (kill runaway queries, require partition filters). The bill is a scan-volume problem — every TB scanned is a line item
Switch to a cheaper warehouse
scenarios.why: Warehouse cost = bytes scanned (roughly), so the bill IS the architecture: 30 analysts × full 50TB scans with no pruning, plus 12x recomputation of the same aggregates. Partitioning on filter columns enables pruning (queries read GBs not TBs); the shared mart converts 12 recomputations into 1; cost attribution makes teams feel their scans. Vendor-switching without fixing scan patterns just moves the bill.
scenarios.hint: What is the warehouse actually billing you for — and what multiplies it 12 times?
objectives: Cut warehouse cost via pruning, shared marts, and attribution
evidence: Compute the daily recomputation waste: 12 models × same aggregate

scenarios.title: Commitment Decisions
scenarios.situation: The cloud vendor offers 40% off compute with a 1-year commitment ($500K). Your usage last year was $700K on-demand, growing 30%/year. Finance loves the discount; engineering worries about lock-in and over-commitment.
scenarios.prompt: How do you decide the commitment level?
choices: Commit the full $500K — 40% off is 40% off
Don't commit anything — flexibility is worth more

Commit to the FLOOR, not the forecast: cover the stable baseline (the minimum monthly usage over the last 6 months — say $300K) with committed capacity, leave growth and spikes on-demand. Over-commitment wastes more than under-commitment saves (unused commitment is 100% loss vs on-demand's 0% discount). Revisit quarterly as the floor rises
Commit based on next year's projected total
scenarios.why: Commitment math is asymmetric: unused committed dollars are pure waste (you pay whether you use them), while on-demand for the excess just misses the discount. The historical FLOOR is the safe commitment — it's usage you'd buy anyway. Growth projections are hopes; the floor is evidence. Quarterly revisits ratchet the commitment up as the floor provably rises. Finance gets most of the discount with none of the waste risk.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the committed dollars if growth stalls — vs what happens to on-demand dollars?
objectives: Size commitments to the usage floor, not the forecast
evidence: Explain the asymmetry between over- and under-commitment

scenarios.title: Unit Economics
scenarios.situation: Leadership asks: 'What does our data platform cost per order processed?' You have the $90K/month warehouse bill, $40K/month streaming, $25K/month orchestration — but no mapping to business units. The orders team says 'data is infrastructure, don't charge us.'
scenarios.prompt: How do you build unit economics, and how do you handle the pushback?
choices: Build attributed unit economics: tag costs by pipeline/team (query attribution, per-pipeline compute tags), compute cost per order per pipeline, and present it as DECISION data not a bill ('the fraud pipeline costs $0.02/order; the recommendations pipeline costs $0.15/order — is the lift worth it?'). The pushback dissolves when it's framed as ROI input, not chargeback — nobody argues with knowing their pipeline's efficiency
Divide total cost by total orders — $X per order, done
Don't do unit economics — it creates political fights
Charge each team an equal share
scenarios.why: Blended averages hide the decisions: $0.02/order fraud detection vs $0.15/order recommendations are different ROI conversations. Attribution (tags, query logs) makes the numbers real; framing as decision-support ('is the lift worth $0.15?') instead of chargeback removes the political threat. Teams that see their own efficiency numbers self-optimize — the 'infrastructure, don't charge us' objection is really fear of an arbitrary bill, which attribution eliminates.
scenarios.hint: What decision does 'cost per order' enable that a $155K total doesn't?
objectives: Build attributed unit economics framed as ROI input
evidence: Write the unit-economics question for one pipeline

scenarios.title: The FinOps Conversation
scenarios.situation: FinOps flags your team's $155K/month spend, up 60% in 6 months. The data grew 40% and you launched 2 new pipelines. FinOps wants a 20% cut 'across the board'. Your pipelines are all SLO-bound.
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle the across-the-board cut demand?
choices: Reframe with data: show the spend decomposed (growth-driven vs new-pipeline vs waste), propose the cut from the WASTE slice (idle clusters, unpruned scans, over-provisioned dev) with specific items totaling 20%, and convert the conversation from 'cut 20%' to 'here's our efficiency plan with dates'. Across-the-board cuts punish efficient pipelines equally with wasteful ones — itemized waste removal gets the same dollars without SLO damage
Accept the 20% cut and degrade the SLOs quietly
Refuse — SLOs are non-negotiable
Blame data growth
scenarios.why: Across-the-board cuts are FinOps' opening bid, not analysis — they assume uniform waste. The decomposed spend (with the waste items named and priced) gives them their 20% from actual inefficiency while protecting SLO-bound work. The efficiency plan with dates converts an adversarial cut into a joint program. 'Refuse' burns the relationship; 'accept and degrade quietly' burns trust when SLOs slip.
scenarios.hint: What fraction of the 60% growth is waste — and can you name it in dollars?
objectives: Convert cut demands into itemized efficiency plans
evidence: Decompose the 60% growth into its three drivers

scenarios.title: Finding the Waste
scenarios.situation: You're asked to find 30% savings in the data platform without touching production SLOs. Where do you look first? The platform: dev/staging environments, old snapshots, orphaned tables, scheduled jobs, and storage tiers.
scenarios.prompt: What is the waste-hunting order?
choices: Hunt in waste-density order: (1) orphaned resources (tables nobody queries in 90 days, old snapshots, dead pipelines still scheduled — pure waste, zero risk to cut), (2) environment hygiene (dev/staging running 24/7, oversized dev warehouses), (3) storage tiering (cold data on hot storage), (4) THEN production efficiency. The first three are risk-free savings; production tuning risks SLOs for smaller gains
Start with production query optimization — it's the biggest spend
Delete everything older than a year
It's impossible without SLO impact
scenarios.why: Waste-density ordering maximizes safe savings: orphaned resources are 100% waste (nobody reads them — verify with query logs first), dev environments running nights/weekends are pure idle, cold data on hot storage is a tiering error. These three routinely yield 20-30% with zero production risk. Production optimization comes last because it's the only category that CAN hurt SLOs — and it's usually the smallest waste slice anyway.
scenarios.hint: Which savings require zero changes to anything anyone uses?
objectives: Hunt waste in risk order: orphans, environments, tiering, then prod
evidence: Name the query-log check that proves a table is orphaned

scenarios.title: Storage Tiering
scenarios.situation: You store 2PB total: 100TB queried daily, 400TB queried monthly, 1.5PB almost never (compliance/audit). It's all on hot storage at $23/TB/month = $46K/month. The CFO asks why storage costs more than compute.
scenarios.prompt: What is the tiering strategy?
choices: Tier by access pattern: hot (100TB daily) stays on fast storage, warm (400TB monthly) moves to infrequent-access (retrieval in minutes, ~half price), cold (1.5PB compliance) moves to archive (retrieval in hours, ~1/10th price). Automate with lifecycle policies (object age + access tracking), and price the retrieval: archive saves $20K/month; a compliance retrieval costs $500 — the math overwhelmingly favors tiering. Deletion needs legal sign-off; tiering doesn't
Delete the 1.5PB — nobody queries it
Compress everything — that'll fix it
It's fine — storage is cheap
scenarios.why: The access pattern IS the tiering spec: daily-query data needs milliseconds, compliance data needs existence. Archive storage at ~1/10th price turns the 1.5PB from $34K/month to ~$3K — the single biggest line item in the savings plan. Lifecycle policies automate it (no manual moves); retrieval pricing makes the trade-off explicit and tiny. 'Nobody queries it' ≠ deletable (compliance), but it does mean archivable.
scenarios.hint: What does the 1.5PB actually need — millisecond access, or just existence?
objectives: Tier storage by access pattern with lifecycle automation
evidence: Compute the monthly savings of archiving the 1.5PB

lessons.title: Data Modeling — Core concepts
concepts: Star schema: fact table at the finest grain (one row per sale line, with measures like amount/qty) surrounded by denormalized dimensions (product with category hierarchy inline, date with month/quarter).

Facts and dimensions: conformed dimensions are shared, consistent dimensions across facts: one date dimension, one customer dimension, same keys and definitions everywhere. Degenerate dimensions (transaction numbers, order IDs with no attributes) stay as plain columns on the fact — they're dimensional but need no table.

Slowly changing dimensions: building conformed dimensions is the core data-warehouse discipline — it's what turns marts into a warehouse. All measures must be additive at that grain; all dimensions must attach at that grain.

Fact grain: declare the grain ('one row per order line'), enforce it in the load, and build separate fact tables for different grains (orders vs lines) rather than mixing. Without the bridge you'd either duplicate fact rows (double-counting) or lose the split.

Junk dimensions: denormalized dimensions trade storage (cheap) for fewer joins (fast). Junk dimension: one table with a row per observed flag combination, referenced by a single surrogate key — 12 flags become 1 key, and combo filters become dimension lookups.

lessons.title: Warehouses & Lakes — Core concepts
concepts: Lakehouse table formats (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi) layer ACID transactions, schema enforcement/evolution, and time travel over Parquet/ORC files on object storage — warehouse reliability at lake storage cost.
File formats: discipline: partition by common filter columns (usually date), target ~100 MB–1 GB per partition/file, compact small files (OPTIMIZE/VACUUM in lakehouse formats).

Columnar storage: parquet is columnar: values of one column are stored together — compressed (same-type data compresses well), with min/max statistics per row group enabling predicate pushdown (skip whole row groups).
Partitioning prunes data (skip irrelevant date partitions), but each partition is metadata + files.
Small-files problem: too fine (hourly for small data, or high-cardinality keys) → small-files problem: slow listings, metastore bloat, poor compression.

example.code:
SELECT * FROM orders TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-10-01 09:00:00';
-- or VERSION AS OF 42
example.walkthrough: Lakehouse time travel queries historical snapshots (TIMESTAMP/VERSION AS OF) — inspect the 9 AM state, diff against now, and either roll back (RESTORE) or surgically fix. No backup restore, no data loss window beyond the bad writes. Retention (e.g., 30 days of history) bounds the lookback.

pitfalls: Common trap: row formats are better for aggregations.
Common trap: partitioning doesn't matter with Parquet.
Common trap: medallion means three databases.
Common trap: copy the warehouse to the app database nightly.

lessons.title: Streaming — Core concepts
concepts: Event time = when the event occurred (the business truth); processing time = when the pipeline saw it (an accident of connectivity). Lambda: batch layer (accurate, high latency) + speed layer (approximate, low latency), merged at query time — two systems to maintain, logic drift risk.
Processing time: correct windows use event time; watermarks ('we've seen all events up to T, modulo lateness') let the system close windows while tolerating late data.
Watermarks: streaming buys freshness at the cost of operational complexity (state management, watermarks, exactly-once, 24/7 on-call).

lessons.title: Quality & Governance — Core concepts
concepts: Data quality tests: a data contract is the API of data: schema, semantics ('revenue = recognized, net of refunds'), quality SLAs, and change policy (how breaking changes are announced/versioned).

dbt tests: data tests run inside the pipeline: schema tests (expected columns/types), volume tests (row count within bounds — catches partial loads), distribution tests (null rates, distinct counts), freshness tests (max timestamp recency).
Data contracts: on failure: halt or quarantine the batch (don't publish bad data downstream), alert with context. 'Data downtime' = periods the data isn't usable, measured like uptime.

Data lineage: lineage (ideally column-level, captured automatically from pipeline code/SQL parsing) answers: 'what breaks if I change X?' and 'why is this dashboard wrong?' (trace back to the source).

PII governance: pipeline PII discipline: classify at ingestion (tag PII columns), mask/tokenize for analytics and non-prod (analysts get hashed IDs, not emails), enforce column-level access, and design for deletion (right-to-erasure must propagate through bronze→gold and backups — hard with immutable logs, so minimize PII upstream).

lessons.title: Data Engineering — Core concepts
concepts: ELT vs ETL is about where compute lives: ELT lands raw data in the warehouse and transforms with SQL — keeping history and adapting to schema drift; ETL transforms before loading, which suits strict contracts and smaller targets.
Airflow orchestrates, it doesn't process: DAGs declare tasks and dependencies, operators do the work, sensors wait for the outside world — and every task should be idempotent so retries are safe.

Spark is lazy: transformations build a plan, actions trigger execution — so performance work (partitioning, broadcast joins, avoiding shuffles) happens at the plan level, not by tuning the cluster first.
Model for the query pattern: star schemas (facts plus conformed dimensions) serve analytics well, and SCD Type 2 preserves history with effective dates when 'what did we know then?' matters.
Streaming correctness rests on event time: watermarks bound how long you wait for late data, and exactly-once comes from idempotent sinks — not from hoping nothing fails.

example.code:
spark-submit --master yarn --deploy-mode cluster \
  --conf spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=200 \
  --conf spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold=10485760 \
  jobs/nightly_events.py
example.walkthrough: This launches the job on the cluster with 200 shuffle partitions to spread the work evenly, and raises the broadcast threshold so small dimension tables join locally instead of shuffling gigabytes.

pitfalls: Common trap: letting a new DAG backfill years of history — set catchup=False or choose the start date deliberately.
Common trap: one giant partition from a skewed key, leaving a single task running for hours while the rest idle — salt or repartition hot keys.
Common trap: non-idempotent writes plus retries — the classic double-count; design every task to be safely re-runnable.
Common trap: a watermark tighter than actual lateness — late events are silently dropped and totals never reconcile.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Data Engineering move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: Anatomy of Data Modeling
concepts: Data Modeling is a multi-step process within Data Modeling: trace the full sequence from initiation to completion
See it as a journey: identify the trigger, follow each handoff, watch state change at every step
Every step depends on the previous — a failure at any point breaks the chain. Map these dependencies
Connect Data Modeling to the broader Data Modeling ecosystem — nothing operates in isolation

example.code:
Step 1: Initiation
  Data Modeling begins — what triggers it?

Step 2: Processing
  Data flows through — what transforms it?

Step 3: Handoff
  Result passes to next system — what is the interface?

Step 4: Completion
  Final state reached — how do you verify?
example.walkthrough: Apply the four-step anatomy method to Data Modeling. Draw it as a flowing sequence, not a static diagram.

pitfalls: Treating Data Modeling as an isolated component instead of part of a living flow
Skipping the dependency mapping — not asking 'what does this step need from the previous?'
Memorizing the steps without understanding WHY each one exists
lessons.try_it: Whiteboard the full Data Modeling flow from memory. Label every handoff and dependency.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: The study order is deliberate — follow it: Start Here first, then work each domain in listed order. Domains unlock as you demonstrate mastery, because Data Engineering Interview topics build on each other.
What 'terminal' means: the Terminal tab is a real shell where labs run. Every lab command executes there — you learn by doing, not by reading about doing.
Lessons teach concepts with a worked example, pitfalls, and a try-it prompt. Scenarios test judgment under realistic pressure. Labs prove you can execute. The mock assessment ties it all together.
Knowledge checks verify understanding before a lesson counts complete — you cannot click through. Spaced repetition resurfaces weak areas automatically.
Your progress syncs as you work. A domain is mastered when lessons are verified, scenarios answered, and labs completed.

example.code:
Day 1: complete all 4 Start Here lessons
Day 2-3: first two content domains (lessons + scenarios)
Day 4+: one domain per day, labs each evening
Final 3 days: mock assessment runs + capstone build
example.walkthrough: This order exists because later domains assume earlier vocabulary. Skipping ahead creates gaps that the mock assessment will expose — painfully. Trust the sequence.

pitfalls: Skimming lessons without attempting the knowledge check — verification is the learning, not a gate to dodge.
Doing scenarios before reading the domain lessons — scenarios assume the concepts; you will guess instead of reason.
Ignoring the Terminal labs — hands-on execution is what separates passing from failing on performance-based questions.
lessons.try_it: Open the Terminal tab now and type `whoami`. That is the smallest possible lab — you just proved the environment works.

lessons.title: Data Engineering Interview Exam Strategy
concepts: Data Engineering Interview tests applied judgment more than memorization. Roughly a third of questions are scenario-based: read the situation, eliminate distractors, pick the BEST answer — not merely a correct one.
Performance-based questions (PBQs) simulate real tasks: drag-and-drop, CLI output analysis, log reading. The labs in this bootcamp are PBQ rehearsal — treat every lab as exam practice.
Time budget: divide total minutes by question count before you start, then check the clock every 20 questions. Flag hard questions and move on — a stuck minute is a lost minute.
Elimination first: cross out the two obviously wrong choices, then compare the remaining two against the question's constraints (cheapest? most secure? first step?).
Never leave a question blank. There is no penalty for wrong answers — an educated guess beats an empty one every time.

example.code:
Q: 'A user reports... Which should you do FIRST?'
  → The word FIRST is the whole question.
  → Eliminate any choice that is a later step.
  → Among the rest, pick the diagnostic before the fix.
example.walkthrough: Exam writers love FIRST, BEST, MOST, and LEAST. Those words change the answer even when the scenario looks identical. Read the actual question stem twice — once for the story, once for the ask.

pitfalls: Answering the scenario instead of the question — the story is context; the final sentence is the task.
Changing answers on review without new evidence — first instincts outperform second-guessing statistically.
Memorizing acronyms without understanding the process behind them — PBQs punish surface knowledge.
lessons.try_it: Take any scenario in this bootcamp, cover the choices, and write what the question is really asking in one sentence before looking at options.

lessons.title: Study System: Spaced Repetition That Sticks
concepts: Forgetting is the default — plan for it. Review a domain's key concepts at expanding intervals: 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 14 days. Each successful recall strengthens the memory trace.
Active recall beats re-reading: close the lesson and explain the concept aloud in your own words. If you cannot explain it, you do not know it yet.
Interleave domains instead of block-studying one: mix scenarios from two domains in a session. Exams mix topics — your practice should too.
The Feynman check: after each lesson, write a 3-sentence explanation a junior could follow. Vague sentences reveal vague understanding.
Weekly rhythm: 2 domains + one pipeline build per week; system design practice at week 4 and 6.

example.code:
Session template (90 min):
  0-10   warm-up: 5 flashcards / quick recalls
  10-50  new domain: lessons + knowledge checks
  50-75  scenarios from today + one older domain (interleaving)
  75-90  one terminal lab, then 3-sentence Feynman writes
example.walkthrough: Ninety focused minutes beat four distracted hours. The template above is engineered for retention, not seat time — protect the lab block, it is where skills become reflexes.

pitfalls: Re-reading notes and calling it studying — recognition is not recall; the exam tests recall.
Cramming new domains the night before — sleep consolidates memory; an all-nighter trades retention for exhaustion.
Skipping the Feynman write — it feels slow, but it is the fastest diagnostic of real understanding.
lessons.try_it: Do one Feynman write right now: explain in 3 sentences what a bootcamp 'domain' is and why the order matters.

lessons.title: Systems Thinking: Your Unfair Advantage
concepts: Exams and interviews reward systems thinkers: people who trace a request end-to-end instead of reciting isolated facts. This bootcamp trains that explicitly in the Systems Anatomy domain.
The four-step method: (1) see the whole in context, (2) cut it open to reveal layers, (3) walk the process step-by-step, (4) pull apart into labeled pieces.
Every troubleshooting scenario here is a systems trace in disguise: start from the symptom, walk backward through dependencies, find where the expected flow diverges from reality.
In interviews, narrate the journey: 'the request starts here, then…' — hiring managers hear senior-level thinking when you trace instead of define.
The Systems Anatomy explorer in Visuals lets you step through living systems click by click. Use it before each domain's scenarios.

example.code:
Weak answer: 'DNS resolves names to IPs.'
Strong answer: 'The stub resolver asks the recursive resolver, which walks root → TLD → authoritative, caching at each level — that is why the first lookup is slow and the second is instant.'
example.walkthrough: One narrated journey demonstrates more competence than ten memorized definitions. Practice this voice in every scenario's 'why' explanation — read them aloud.

pitfalls: Defining terms instead of tracing flows when asked 'how does X work?'
Jumping to fixes before mapping the system — fixes applied to the wrong layer waste time and credibility.
Treating each domain as separate — the mock assessment deliberately chains them; practice connecting domains now.
lessons.try_it: Open the Systems Anatomy domain and step through one full system in the explorer before your first study session.

lessons.title: Mock Assessment Briefing: Rules of Engagement
concepts: The mock simulates Data Engineering Interview conditions: timed, mixed-domain, no hints, one shot per question. Treat it as the real exam — same chair, same focus, no phone.
Scoring mirrors the real exam's weighting: scenario judgment counts more than recall. A wrong answer on a multi-step scenario costs more than a missed definition.
Run the mock only after all domains show 80%+ mastery. Running it early wastes its diagnostic value — it is a measuring instrument, not a study tool.
After each run, the review breaks down misses by domain. Your next study block targets exactly those domains — the mock tells you where to aim.
Two full runs minimum: the first finds gaps, the second confirms they are closed. A passing second run is your green light.

example.code:
Mock protocol:
  1. Silence notifications, full-screen the bootcamp
  2. Note start time; budget per-question time on paper
  3. Answer every question — no blanks
  4. Flag-and-move on stuck questions; return with fresh eyes
  5. Review the domain breakdown before any celebration
example.walkthrough: The mock's value is the breakdown, not the score. A 68% with a clear miss-map beats a lucky 82% — the map tells you exactly what to study next.

pitfalls: Peeking at notes mid-mock — it inflates the score and destroys the diagnostic.
Running the mock as a first activity — without domain mastery it only measures unpreparedness.
Ignoring the domain breakdown — the score is trivia; the miss-map is the study plan.
lessons.try_it: Check your domain mastery percentages now. List any domain under 80% — those are your pre-mock targets.

lessons.title: Reviewing a Mock Run: Turning Misses into Mastery
concepts: For every missed question, classify the error: knowledge gap (never learned it), application gap (knew it, misapplied it), or reading error (misread the ask). Each type needs a different fix.
Knowledge gaps go back to the domain lesson — re-read, re-verify, Feynman-write. Application gaps need more scenarios, not more reading. Reading errors need the exam-strategy lesson again.
Keep an error log: question topic, error type, correct reasoning in one sentence. Patterns emerge fast — three 'reading errors' in a row is a process problem, not a knowledge problem.
Re-test missed topics within 48 hours with fresh scenarios. A corrected mistake that is not re-tested is a mistake waiting to recur.
Your second mock run should show misses migrating: fewer knowledge gaps, zero repeated reading errors. That migration is the signal you are ready.

example.code:
Error log entry:
  Q: firewall rule order scenario → chose 'deny' before 'allow'
  Type: application gap (knew rule order, misapplied under time pressure)
  Fix: 5 more firewall scenarios, timed
  Correct reasoning: 'First match wins — the allow had to precede the deny.'
example.walkthrough: Do not just re-read the explanation and move on. The error log forces you to name the failure mode — and named failures are fixable failures.

pitfalls: Re-reading explanations passively — recognition feels like learning but evaporates under pressure.
Studying only the missed topics and neglecting maintenance review of strong ones — strengths decay too.
Taking the second mock too soon — give fixes 48 hours and a re-test cycle first.
lessons.try_it: Create your error log file now (paper or notes app). You will need it after your first mock run.

lessons.title: Capstone Plan: What You Will Build and Why
concepts: Employers and examiners trust demonstrated skill over claimed knowledge. Your capstone is a working artifact — something you can screenshare and narrate in under 10 minutes.
Pick ONE project from the list below. Depth beats breadth: a single polished build outperforms three half-finished ones.
Scope it to finish in 2–3 focused sessions. If it needs more, cut features — a complete small project beats an ambitious pile of parts.
Document as you go: every decision gets a one-line reason. That log becomes your interview narration script.
Done means: it works end-to-end, you can demo it live, and you can explain every part without notes.

example.code:
Pick your project:
  1. Streaming Pipeline — an end-to-end streaming pipeline with monitoring
  2. Lakehouse Build — a partitioned, optimized lakehouse with cost analysis
  3. Data Quality Framework — automated validation with alerting
example.walkthrough: Choose the project that scares you slightly — that is where the growth is. But cap the scope ruthlessly: you must finish.

pitfalls: Starting two projects and finishing neither — pick one, finish it, then consider a second.
Building without documenting — the demo narration is half the value; no log means no story.
Gold-plating instead of finishing — ship the working core first, polish only if time remains.
lessons.try_it: Write your one-paragraph project selection rationale now: which project, why it fits your goals, and what 'done' looks like.

lessons.title: Build Log: Decisions, Dead Ends, and Proof
concepts: Keep a build log with timestamps: what you tried, what happened, what you changed. Dead ends are valuable — they prove you debugged, not just followed a tutorial.
For each component, record: purpose (one line), how it works (three lines), how you tested it (one command or check).
Screenshot or record key milestones. A 60-second screen recording of the working project is worth more than a page of description.
Version your work: even a simple dated folder structure beats a single 'final' file. Show the progression.
The log is not overhead — it IS the deliverable's companion. Interviewers ask 'tell me about a challenge'; your log hands you the answer.

example.code:
Build log entry:
  14:32 — Tried X config; service failed with error Y
  14:47 — Found cause: Z was misconfigured (docs said A, reality was B)
  15:05 — Fixed; verified with [test command]; works end-to-end
example.walkthrough: Write the log as you go, not after. Memory lies; timestamps do not. Future-you (in the interview) will thank present-you.

pitfalls: Writing the log from memory at the end — you will forget the dead ends, which are the best stories.
Skipping the 'how I tested it' line — untested claims collapse under the first interview question.
No recordings — a live demo can fail; a recording is bulletproof backup.
lessons.try_it: Create your build log file now with today's date and your project title as the header.

lessons.title: Demo Day: Narrating Your Build in 10 Minutes
concepts: Structure the demo: problem (1 min) → architecture (2 min) → live walkthrough (5 min) → lessons learned (2 min). Rehearse it twice, timed.
Narrate the systems journey: 'a request starts here, flows through…' — the Systems Anatomy voice. Show you understand the whole, not just the parts you typed.
Prepare for three hard questions: 'why this approach over X?', 'what breaks at scale?', 'what would you do differently?'. Write your answers in advance.
Lead with the working demo, not slides. Working software presented live beats any deck.
End with the repo/README link and offer to walk through the code. Make it effortless for them to verify your work.

example.code:
Demo script skeleton:
  'I built [X] because [problem]. It works by [3-step journey].
   Watch: [live action]. The tricky part was [challenge] —
   I solved it by [approach]. Code and docs are at [link].'
example.walkthrough: Rehearsal is non-negotiable. A polished 10-minute demo signals preparation, communication skill, and genuine ownership — exactly what hiring managers screen for.

pitfalls: Wing the demo — 'let me just show you' without a plan wastes the moment.
Hiding the challenges — the dead ends and fixes are what prove real engineering happened.
No backup plan — have the recording ready in case live demo gods are unkind.
lessons.try_it: Draft your three hard-question answers now, before you build. They will sharpen your design decisions.

lessons.title: Roles That Hire Data Engineering Skills
concepts: The roles: Data Engineer, Analytics Engineer, Platform Engineer (Data). Read 10 job postings and extract the repeated requirements — that list is your real syllabus.
Titles vary by company; skills cluster by function. Map postings to skill clusters (not titles) to see what the market actually buys.
Entry points differ: some roles hire on certification + projects, others on portfolio + interviews. Know your target's gate before optimizing for it.
Salary bands follow scarcity + impact: specialized + revenue-adjacent pays more. Position yourself at that intersection deliberately.
Track the market quarterly: which skills are rising in postings? Your learning backlog should follow the demand signal.

example.code:
Posting analysis template:
  Role: ___
  Repeated requirements (3+ postings): ___
  Nice-to-haves: ___
  My gaps: ___ → study priority
example.walkthrough: The job posting is the employer's requirements doc. Analyze it like one — systematically, not hopefully.

pitfalls: Chasing titles instead of skill clusters — the same skills hide under five different titles.
Ignoring the 'repeated requirements' — what 8/10 postings demand is the real bar.
No gap analysis — studying without knowing your gaps is motion without direction.
lessons.try_it: Pull 5 postings for your target role now. List the top 5 repeated requirements.

lessons.title: Resume & Projects That Get Callbacks
concepts: Resumes get 30 seconds: lead with a skills line matching the posting's keywords, then 3-4 bullets per role with quantified outcomes (not duties).
Projects beat buzzwords: one deployed, documented project outweighs a paragraph of claimed skills. Link the repo AND the live demo.
Tailor per application: mirror the posting's language for the top 5 requirements. ATS filters are literal — 'PostgreSQL' does not match 'postgres' in dumb parsers.
The capstone in this bootcamp IS your resume project: finish it, document it, link it. That single line does more work than any certification bullet.
GitHub profile hygiene: pinned repos with READMEs, green contribution squares, no empty forks. Recruiters do click through.

example.code:
Bullet formula: [Action verb] + [what] + [scale] + [outcome]
  Weak: 'Responsible for databases.'
  Strong: 'Migrated 2TB analytics DB to Postgres; cut query p95 40%; zero-downtime cutover.'
example.walkthrough: Every bullet must answer: what did you do, at what scale, to what effect? Duties describe jobs; outcomes get interviews.

pitfalls: Skill lists without evidence — every claimed skill needs a project or role bullet backing it.
One generic resume for all applications — tailoring is the highest-ROI 20 minutes in job hunting.
No links — a project without a URL might as well not exist.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite your weakest resume bullet using the formula above. Quantify something.

lessons.title: Interview Loops: What Actually Happens
concepts: Typical loop: recruiter screen (15 min, fit + comp) → technical screen (45-60 min, live problems) → onsite/virtual loop (3-5 rounds: technical depth, system design, behavioral) → offer.
Technical screens test thinking aloud: narrate your approach before coding/querying. Silence is scored as stuck; structured thinking is scored as senior.
Behavioral rounds use STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) — prepare 5 stories covering: conflict, failure, leadership, ambiguity, and impact. Quantify results.
Questions YOU ask matter: 'what does success look like in 90 days?' and 'what's the hardest problem the team faces?' signal seriousness. Never ask nothing.
Follow up within 24 hours: thank-you note referencing something specific from the conversation. Small effort, real signal.

example.code:
STAR story skeleton:
  S: 'Our deploy pipeline broke weekly...'
  T: 'I owned stabilizing it in Q3...'
  A: 'I added staged rollouts + runbook...'
  R: 'Deploys went from 60% to 99% success; on-call pages dropped 70%.'
example.walkthrough: Prepare stories, not scripts: know your 5 STAR stories cold enough to adapt to any behavioral question. Rehearse aloud twice.

pitfalls: No questions for them — reads as disinterest; always ask two.
Rambling technical answers — structure: approach first, then detail, then verify.
Badmouthing past employers — the interviewer hears how you will talk about THEM.
lessons.try_it: Draft one STAR story now using the skeleton. Time it — aim for 90 seconds.

lessons.title: The Data Engineering Tool Landscape
concepts: Tools cluster by job-to-be-done, not by vendor. Learn the categories first, then pick one tool per category deeply — depth in one beats surface in five.
The 80/20 rule: 20% of each tool's features cover 80% of real work. Master the core workflow before exploring the edges.
Free/open tiers are enough to learn: every major platform has a free tier or community edition sufficient for portfolio projects. Never pay to learn the basics.
Tool churn is constant; fundamentals are stable. SQL outlives every BI tool; TCP/IP outlives every cloud console. Invest in fundamentals first.

For Data Engineering, the essential categories:
  Processing: Spark/Flink
  Orchestration: Airflow
  Storage: Delta/Iceberg
  Streaming: Kafka

example.code:
Learning order:
  1. One tool per category, core workflow only
  2. Build the capstone using exactly these tools
  3. Add a second tool per category only when a job posting demands it
example.walkthrough: Resist tool tourism: each new tool costs weeks. The portfolio proves depth; the resume lists breadth honestly.

pitfalls: Learning 5 tools shallowly instead of 2 deeply — interviews probe depth.
Paying for premium tiers to learn — free tiers cover 90% of learning needs.
Chasing every new release — fundamentals first; novelty second.
lessons.try_it: List your one-tool-per-category stack now. Identify any category where you have zero depth — that is your next lab.

lessons.title: Workflows: Connecting the Tools
concepts: Tools in isolation are trivia; workflows are skill. The professional unit is the end-to-end flow: ingest → transform → validate → deliver — across YOUR tool stack.
