Document your workflows as runbooks: trigger, steps, verification, rollback. A runbook turns personal knowledge into team capability.
Automate the toil, not the judgment: repetitive steps get scripted; decisions stay human. If you do it weekly, automate it.
Version everything: code, configs, queries, dashboards. 'Final_v2_ACTUAL' is not version control — git is.
The workflow IS the portfolio piece: 'here is my pipeline, here is the runbook, here is the monitoring' — that sentence hires.

example.code:
Runbook skeleton:
  Trigger: ___ (schedule/event/manual)
  Steps: 1.___ 2.___ 3.___
  Verify: ___ (how do you know it worked?)
  Rollback: ___ (how do you undo it?)
  Owner: ___  Last tested: ___
example.walkthrough: Write the runbook BEFORE automating: it forces you to understand the workflow well enough to hand it to someone else.

pitfalls: Automating before documenting — you encode confusion at machine speed.
No verification step — a workflow without a check is a hope with extra steps.
No rollback plan — the first failure without one teaches this lesson permanently.
lessons.try_it: Write a runbook for one workflow you do regularly, using the skeleton above.

lessons.title: Pipeline System Design: The Interview
concepts: DE system design interviews test trade-offs, not tools: 'design a pipeline for 10TB/day of clickstream' — they want to hear you reason about batch vs streaming, exactly-once, and backfill.
Start with requirements: volume, velocity, latency SLA, correctness needs (exactly-once?), retention, consumers. Five minutes of questions beats fifty minutes of wrong architecture.
Sketch the standard shape: ingest (Kafka/Kinesis) → stream or batch processing (Spark/Flink) → storage (lakehouse) → serving (warehouse/marts) → orchestration + monitoring around everything.
Name the hard parts explicitly: late data, schema evolution, backfills, exactly-once sinks, cost. Interviewers promote candidates who volunteer the difficulties.
Trade-off language wins: 'I'd choose X because [reason], accepting [downside]; if latency tightened to seconds I'd switch to Y.' Decisions with reasons beat tool lists.

example.code:
Prompt: 'Design clickstream ingestion, 10TB/day, 5-min freshness.'
  Ask: exactly-once needed? (billing → yes; dashboards → no)
  Sketch: Kafka → Flink (5-min windows) → Iceberg lake → dbt marts
  Hard parts: late events (watermarks), backfill (replay), cost (partition by day)
example.walkthrough: The interview is a thinking-aloud exercise. Requirements first, sketch second, trade-offs throughout, hard parts volunteered.

pitfalls: Listing tools without requirements — 'use Kafka, Spark, Airflow' answers nothing.
Ignoring the hard parts — late data and backfills are where seniors separate from juniors.
No trade-off language — every choice has a cost; name it or sound naive.
lessons.try_it: Whiteboard (paper) a 1TB/day batch pipeline in 10 minutes: sources, stages, storage, orchestration. Then list 3 hard parts.

lessons.title: Thinking in Partitions
concepts: Distributed engines split data into partitions and process them in parallel. Performance = (data per partition) × (partition count) tuned so no worker idles and none OOMs.
Target partition size: 128MB–2GB per partition for Spark. Too small = scheduling overhead dominates; too large = OOM and stragglers. Repartition deliberately at stage boundaries.
Skew is the killer: one key with 90% of data means one worker does 90% of the work while 99 idle. Detect via stage skew metrics; fix with salting (add random prefix, aggregate twice).
Shuffles (repartitioning by key: joins, groupBys) are the expensive operation — network + disk + sort. Minimize shuffles: broadcast small tables, pre-partition, avoid UDFs that block optimization.
Narrow vs wide transformations: map/filter are narrow (no shuffle, fast); groupBy/join are wide (shuffle, slow). Read the query plan for 'Exchange' nodes — each is a shuffle to justify.

example.code:
Skewed join: events (10B rows) JOIN users (10M rows) on user_id; 1% of users = 60% of events.
  Fix: salt the heavy keys —
    events: CONCAT(user_id, '-', RAND(10)) as salted
    users: explode to 10 salted copies
    join on salted key, then strip salt and re-aggregate.
  Result: work spreads across workers; straggler eliminated.
example.walkthrough: If you remember one thing: data distribution decides performance. Uniform partitions fly; skewed partitions crawl — and skew hides in innocent-looking keys.

pitfalls: Default partition counts on huge data — 200 partitions for 10TB means 50GB partitions: OOM city.
Broadcasting a 'small' table that is actually 2GB — broadcast joins have limits; check the size first.
UDFs in hot paths — they block Catalyst optimization; prefer native functions.
lessons.try_it: Explain salting to a rubber duck: why two aggregations, and what the random prefix accomplishes.

lessons.title: Exactly-Once: What It Really Takes
concepts: Exactly-once has two halves: no duplicate processing AND no duplicate effects. Idempotent sinks (upserts by key) make the second half achievable even when the first is hard.
Kafka transactions + idempotent producers give EOS within Kafka. End-to-end EOS needs the sink's cooperation: transactional writes or idempotent upserts keyed on the event ID.
Checkpoints (Flink) / offsets committed transactionally (Kafka Streams) are the mechanism: state and offsets commit atomically, so a failure replays from a consistent point.
The practical pattern most teams use: at-least-once delivery + idempotent sink (INSERT…ON CONFLICT / MERGE on event_id). Simpler than true EOS, correct for most use cases.
Late data policy is part of correctness: watermarks define 'how late is too late'; side outputs rescue the stragglers. Decide the policy before the first incident decides it for you.

example.code:
Billing pipeline (must not double-charge):
  Kafka (transactional) → Flink (checkpointed) → sink: INSERT…ON CONFLICT(event_id) DO NOTHING
  Replay after crash: offsets rewind to checkpoint; duplicates hit the idempotent sink and vanish.
  Correctness argument: duplicates are possible in transport, impossible in effect.
example.walkthrough: Design for idempotent effects and most 'exactly-once' anxiety disappears. The sink key is the unsung hero of streaming correctness.

pitfalls: Claiming exactly-once from the broker alone — the sink completes or breaks the guarantee.
No idempotency key — without a stable event ID, dedup is impossible; ensure producers set one.
Ignoring late data — watermarks are a business decision (how late is still useful?), not just config.
lessons.try_it: Write the idempotent-sink argument for a pipeline you know: what is the key, and what happens on replay?

lessons.title: File Sizing and Partitioning for Lakes
concepts: Small files are the lakehouse tax: 1M tiny files means 1M metadata operations per scan. Target 128MB–1GB per file; compact aggressively (OPTIMIZE/VACUUM in Delta/Iceberg).
Partition by what you filter: date is the classic (queries filter by day), then a low-cardinality dimension (region). Never partition by high-cardinality IDs — 10M partitions is a metadata disaster.
Z-order / sort within partitions by frequent filter columns: co-locates related data so scans skip more files. Partitioning prunes partitions; sorting prunes within them.
Columnar formats (Parquet) + compression (Snappy/ZSTD) + predicate pushdown = scans that read 1% of the data. Verify with file-skipping metrics, not faith.
Cost follows scans: every full-table scan on pay-per-byte warehouses (BigQuery) is a bill. Partition pruning and clustering are cost controls wearing a performance costume.

example.code:
Events table, 5TB, queried by day + country:
  Partition: dt (day) — prunes 364/365 partitions per daily query
  Within: Z-order by country — skips files per country filter
  Files: ~512MB Parquet, Snappy — 10k files, not 10M
  Daily query scans ~14GB instead of 5TB → 350x cheaper on BigQuery
example.walkthrough: Partitioning is a cost decision that looks like a performance decision. Design for the query pattern, measure the skip rate, compact relentlessly.

pitfalls: Partitioning by user_id or timestamp-ms — partition explosion; metadata melts.
Never compacting streaming writes — the lake fills with 1KB files; schedule OPTIMIZE.
Ignoring file-skipping metrics — you cannot tune what you do not measure.
lessons.try_it: For a table you know, write its partitioning scheme and the top-3 query patterns. Do the patterns match the partitions?

lessons.title: Behavioral Rounds for Data Engineers
concepts: DE behavioral themes: a pipeline that broke at 3 AM (ownership), a disagreement on architecture (influence), a data quality incident (rigor), mentoring a junior (leadership). Prepare one story each.
STAR with technical depth: the 'Action' should include the actual technical decision ('chose idempotent upserts over append because...'). Shallow actions read as shallow experience.
The 'tell me about a failure' question is a gift: pick a real incident, own your part, show the systemic fix (monitoring, runbook, test). Growth narratives beat perfection.
Questions to ask them: 'how do you handle backfills?', 'what's the on-call burden?', 'how is data quality owned?' — the answers reveal the team's maturity. Ask like an owner.
Salary bands for DE are wide: know the band for the level (levels.fyi, peers). The technical screen passed = leverage; negotiate the package, not just base.

example.code:
STAR: 3 AM page, revenue pipeline down.
  S: 'PagerDuty 3 AM: daily mart failed, execs need numbers by 8.'
  T: 'Restore by 7 AM without corrupting downstream.'
  A: 'Found the schema change, applied the versioned fix, reran idempotently, verified reconciliation.'
  R: 'Green by 6:15; added contract test + alert — same failure impossible now.'
example.walkthrough: Behavioral rounds test judgment under pressure — exactly what on-call data engineering is. Your incident stories ARE your qualifications; prepare them like code.

pitfalls: No failure story — 'nothing ever broke' reads as inexperienced or dishonest.
Shallow technical actions — 'I fixed it' without the HOW wastes the question.
No questions for them — the on-call and backfill questions reveal team quality; ask them.
lessons.try_it: Write your 3 AM incident story in STAR now. Include the technical decision and the systemic fix.

lessons.title: Spark SQL Deep Dive
concepts: Spark SQL is the primary API now: DataFrames are distributed tables, Catalyst optimizes the plan, Tungsten executes it fast. SQL fluency IS Spark fluency for most work.
Catalyst in 30 seconds: parse → analyze (resolve columns) → optimize (predicate pushdown, projection pruning, join reordering) → physical plan → codegen. EXPLAIN shows the journey.
Read EXPLAIN: look for Exchange (shuffles — minimize), BroadcastHashJoin (good for small tables), SortMergeJoin (default for big-big), and Filter pushdown (predicates near the scan = good).
AQE (Adaptive Query Execution): runtime re-optimization — coalesces shuffle partitions, switches join strategies mid-flight. Enable it; it fixes the plan your static analysis got wrong.
UDFs: the optimization killer — Catalyst can't see inside Python UDFs. Prefer Spark SQL functions; use pandas_udf (vectorized) when you must; avoid row-wise Python UDFs in hot paths.

example.code:
Slow query: 10-min join.
  EXPLAIN: SortMergeJoin with 2TB shuffle on skewed key.
  Fix 1: AQE on → auto-coalesces to sane partitions.
  Fix 2: salt the skewed key (or broadcast if small side).
  Fix 3: replace Python UDF filter with native functions.
  Result: 10 min → 90 sec. The plan told the story.
example.walkthrough: EXPLAIN is the Spark developer's X-ray: learn to read the plan and the optimizer becomes your collaborator instead of your mystery.

pitfalls: Python UDFs in hot paths — Catalyst goes blind; prefer native functions.
Ignoring the plan — 'it's slow' without EXPLAIN is guessing; the plan names the shuffle.
AQE disabled — free runtime optimization; enable it by default.
lessons.try_it: Run EXPLAIN on a join you have. Find the Exchange nodes. Can any be eliminated?

lessons.title: Schema Registry Patterns
concepts: The registry is the contract enforcer: producers register schemas; compatibility checks (BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL) run on every change. Breaking changes fail before deploy.
Compatibility modes: BACKWARD (new readers read old data — most common), FORWARD (old readers read new data), FULL (both). Choose per consumer reality, not ideology.
Subject naming strategies: TopicNameStrategy (one schema per topic — simple) vs RecordNameStrategy (many event types per topic — flexible). The strategy shapes evolution freedom.
Wire format: schema ID embedded in each message (magic byte + ID). Consumers fetch the schema once, cache it. The ID is the version handshake — compact and robust.
Governance: who approves breaking changes? The registry needs a process owner and a deprecation playbook — otherwise it's a speed bump everyone drives around.

example.code:
Breaking change flow:
  Producer PR: renames field → registry check: BACKWARD violated
  → build fails → producer adds new field (nullable) instead
  → consumers migrate → old field deprecated (announced)
  → removed in v3. Zero incidents. The registry earned its keep.
example.walkthrough: Schema registries turn 'hope the consumers handle it' into enforced contracts. The CI check is the cheapest incident prevention in streaming.

pitfalls: No registry — 'we'll coordinate' fails at 3+ teams; the registry scales the coordination.
Wrong compatibility mode — BACKWARD when consumers need FORWARD; match reality.
No deprecation process — fields accumulate forever; version and retire deliberately.
lessons.try_it: Check: does your streaming setup have a registry? If not, write the 3-line proposal for adopting one.

lessons.title: FinOps for Data Teams
concepts: Showback first: tag every job/pipeline with owner and project; publish the cost dashboard. Visibility alone cuts 15-20% — nobody optimizes invisible spend.
The big three levers: right-size compute (most clusters are 2x oversized), kill idle (dev clusters nights/weekends), and fix the scan volume (partitioning, aggregation). In that ROI order.
Unit economics: cost per TB processed, per pipeline run, per dashboard refresh. 'Our pipeline costs $0.42/TB' enables real trade-off conversations with the business.
Commitments for the stable base: savings plans / reserved capacity for the 24/7 baseline (30-50% off). Keep on-demand for spikes — the hybrid is the optimum.
Chargeback (with teeth) vs showback (visibility): start with showback; graduate to chargeback when the culture is ready. The goal is efficient engineering, not accounting theater.

example.code:
Monthly FinOps review:
  Total: $48k (▲3k vs last month — why?)
  Top mover: pipeline X +$5k (backfill ran 3x — one-time, acknowledged)
  Win: dev cluster auto-pause saved $2k
  Action: pipeline Y's scan volume doubled — owner investigating.
  30 minutes, full accountability.
example.walkthrough: FinOps is engineering accountability for money: tag, measure, review, optimize. The monthly review is the control — skip it and costs drift.

pitfalls: No tagging — the bill is a lump; nobody owns anything.
Optimizing before measuring — the top-3 spend list directs effort; start there.
One-time cleanup, no process — costs regrow; the monthly review is the maintenance.
lessons.try_it: List your top 5 cost drivers (or estimate). What is the single highest-ROI optimization?

lessons.title: Dimensional Modeling Deep Dive
concepts: Star vs snowflake: star denormalizes dimensions (fewer joins, faster, simpler); snowflake normalizes (less redundancy, more joins). BI tools prefer star — optimize for the consumer.
Degenerate dimensions: order numbers, transaction IDs live IN the fact table (no dimension table needed). Not every key needs a dimension — know when to stop.
Junk dimensions: combine low-cardinality flags (is_returned, is_gift, payment_type) into one dimension instead of 5 tiny ones. Fewer joins, cleaner model.
Role-playing dimensions: one date dimension playing many roles (order_date, ship_date, return_date) via aliases/views. One table, many perspectives.
The bus matrix: rows = business processes (facts), columns = conformed dimensions. Fill it in a workshop BEFORE modeling — it prevents the 'three customer dimensions' disaster.

example.code:
Bus matrix excerpt:
              | dim_date | dim_customer | dim_product
  fact_orders |    X     |      X       |     X
  fact_returns|    X     |      X       |     X
  fact_inventory|  X     |              |     X
  Shared dimensions = conformed = cross-fact analysis possible.
example.walkthrough: Model in workshops, not alone: the bus matrix session with stakeholders prevents more rework than any modeling technique. The meeting IS the modeling.

pitfalls: One mega-dimension — 200-column dim_customer is unmaintainable; split by change rate.
No bus matrix — three teams build three customer dimensions; integration becomes archaeology.
Snowflaking for purity — BI performance and simplicity beat normalization elegance.
lessons.try_it: Draw a bus matrix for an e-commerce business: 4 facts × 5 dimensions. Mark the conformed ones.

lessons.title: Data Vault for Auditable History
concepts: Data Vault separates: Hubs (business keys — the 'what'), Links (relationships — the 'how connected'), Satellites (descriptive attributes with history — the 'what changed').
The superpower is auditability: every attribute change is a new satellite row with load timestamp. 'What did we know on March 3rd?' is answerable — always.
Hubs use hash keys (MD5 of business key): stable, joinable, source-independent. New source system? Same hub structure — integration without remodeling.
Satellites split by change rate: fast-changing attributes separate from slow ones. Fewer rows written, cleaner history — design for the change pattern.
The cost: more joins, more complexity, steeper learning curve. Use Data Vault where auditability/regulatory history justifies it — not for every mart.

example.code:
Customer hub: H_CUSTOMER (hash of customer_id)
  Link: L_ORDER_CUSTOMER (order ↔ customer)
  Satellites: S_CUSTOMER_PROFILE (name, email — slow change)
              S_CUSTOMER_SEGMENT (segment — fast change)
  Query 'customer as of 2024-06-01': join hubs+links, filter satellites by load_date.
example.walkthrough: Data Vault is the choice when history is a requirement, not a nice-to-have: regulated industries, audit-heavy domains. Know when its power justifies its price.

pitfalls: Data Vault for simple marts — overkill; star schemas serve BI better.
No satellite split strategy — one giant satellite defeats the purpose; split by change rate.
Ignoring the learning curve — the team must understand hubs/links/sats or the model becomes write-only.
lessons.try_it: For a regulated use case you know: sketch hub/link/satellite for 2 entities. Justify the satellite split.

lessons.title: Idempotent Pipelines
concepts: Idempotency: running twice = running once. MERGE/upsert by key, partition overwrite (not append), and transactional writes make reruns safe — and reruns WILL happen.
Partition overwrite pattern: write to date partition atomically (write temp → swap). A failed run leaves yesterday's good data, not half of today's.
Upsert keys must be stable and unique: natural keys preferred; surrogate keys only if truly stable. The key IS the dedup contract — choose it deliberately.
Backfills are reruns at scale: the same idempotency that saves a failed daily run enables historical reprocessing. Design for backfill from day one.
Test idempotency explicitly: run the pipeline twice on test data, diff the outputs. Identical = correct. Different = a bug wearing a pipeline costume.

example.code:
-- Idempotent daily load (Postgres):
INSERT INTO fact_orders (...)
SELECT ... FROM staging
ON CONFLICT (order_id) DO UPDATE SET ...;
-- Run it twice: second run changes nothing. That is the test.
example.walkthrough: Every pipeline will be rerun — failures, backfills, late data. Idempotency turns reruns from incidents into non-events. Build it in, test it explicitly.

pitfalls: Append-only without dedup — every rerun duplicates; the table becomes a lie.
Unstable upsert keys — changing keys break the dedup contract silently.
No rerun test — 'probably idempotent' is not idempotent. Test it.
lessons.try_it: Take one pipeline you know. Is it idempotent? Prove it with the twice-run test (mentally or for real).

lessons.title: Schema Evolution Strategies
concepts: Backward compatible: new consumers read old data (add nullable columns only). Forward compatible: old consumers read new data (never rename/remove without versioning). Know which you guarantee.
The expansion rules: ADD column (nullable) = safe; REMOVE column = breaking; RENAME = breaking (it is remove+add); TYPE WIDENING (int→bigint) = usually safe; NARROWING = breaking.
Schema registry enforcement: producers declare schemas; compatibility checks run in CI. Breaking changes fail the build — the cheapest place to catch them.
Versioned topics/tables for breaking changes: v2 topic alongside v1, dual-write during migration, consumers cut over deliberately. No flag days.
Document the contract: field meanings, nullability, value ranges, ownership. A schema without docs is a rumor — and rumors break pipelines.

example.code:
Need to rename user_id → user_key:
  v1: ADD user_key (nullable), dual-write both
  v2: consumers migrate to user_key (monitored)
  v3: deprecate user_id (announce, wait)
  v4: remove user_id
  Four versions, zero breakage. Boring is beautiful.
example.walkthrough: Schema changes are inevitable; breaking consumers is optional. The versioned, announced, dual-write path is slower — and the only one that works at scale.

pitfalls: Rename-in-place — the fastest way to break every downstream consumer simultaneously.
No registry — 'we will coordinate' does not scale past 3 teams.
Undocumented fields — nullability and meaning are contracts; write them down.
lessons.try_it: Audit one schema change you have seen. Was it backward compatible? What broke, if anything?

lessons.title: Lakehouse Architecture
concepts: Lakehouse = data lake economics + warehouse reliability: open formats (Parquet) on cheap object storage, with ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and time travel via table formats (Delta/Iceberg/Hudi).
The medallion pattern: Bronze (raw, as-landed) → Silver (cleaned, conformed) → Gold (aggregated, business-ready). Each layer has a contract; skipping layers creates mess.
ACID on the lake: transactions prevent the partial-write corruption that plagued old lakes. Time travel (query as-of timestamp) makes debugging and auditing possible.
Schema enforcement vs evolution: block bad writes (enforcement) while allowing planned changes (evolution with compatibility). The lake stays queryable because writes are governed.
One platform, many engines: Spark for batch, Flink for streaming, Trino/DuckDB for SQL — all on the same open tables. No more data silos per engine.

example.code:
E-commerce lakehouse:
  Bronze: raw JSON events (immutable, partitioned by day)
  Silver: cleaned orders/customers (deduped, typed, SCD2)
  Gold: daily_revenue, churn_features (aggregated, tested)
  BI reads Gold; ML reads Silver+Gold; all on Iceberg tables.
example.walkthrough: The lakehouse ends the lake-vs-warehouse war: one copy of data, many engines, governed writes. The medallion layers are the discipline that makes it work.

pitfalls: Skipping Bronze — no raw layer means no reprocessing when logic changes; always land raw.
No schema enforcement — the lake becomes a swamp one bad write at a time.
Gold built directly on Bronze — bypassing Silver duplicates cleaning logic everywhere.
lessons.try_it: Sketch a medallion architecture for a domain you know: what lands in Bronze, what conforms in Silver, what serves from Gold?

lessons.title: Warehouse Performance Patterns
concepts: Distribution/sort keys (Redshift): DISTKEY on the join key (co-located joins), SORTKEY on the filter column (range pruning). Wrong keys = full scans; right keys = magic.
Clustering (BigQuery/Snowflake): automatic micro-partitioning + clustering on filter columns. Declare the clustering; the platform maintains it. Verify with partition pruning metrics.
Result caching: repeated identical queries hit cache (seconds → milliseconds). Dashboards benefit enormously — design for cache hits (stable queries, scheduled refresh).
Concurrency scaling: separate compute for ETL vs BI vs ad-hoc. Noisy ETL should never starve the CEO's dashboard — workload isolation is a reliability control.
The query profile is the truth: EXPLAIN shows the plan; the profile shows reality (spills, skew, scans). Tune from the profile, not from intuition.

example.code:
Slow dashboard diagnosis:
  Profile: 90% time in one join — broadcast of a 2GB 'small' table.
  Fix: distribution key alignment (both sides DISTKEY on join key)
    → co-located join, no broadcast.
  Result: 45s → 3s. The profile named it; the key fixed it.
example.walkthrough: Warehouse performance is data layout + query shape. The profile tells you which; the keys and clustering are the levers. Measure first, always.

pitfalls: Even distribution on everything — the default that optimizes nothing; choose keys deliberately.
No workload isolation — the 3 AM ETL slows the 9 AM dashboard; separate them.
Tuning without the profile — guessing at warehouse scale wastes days.
lessons.try_it: Run EXPLAIN on your slowest query. What is the most expensive operation? What key/clustering would fix it?

lessons.title: Kafka Fundamentals That Matter
concepts: Topics are partitioned logs: append-only, ordered within a partition, retained by time/size. Partitions are the parallelism unit — more partitions, more parallel consumers.
Consumer groups: each partition goes to exactly one consumer in a group. Group of 1 = every message to one consumer; group of N = work shared. Rebalancing on membership change.
Retention is not deletion-on-read: messages persist per retention policy regardless of consumption. Replay is a feature — new consumer groups re-read history.
Keys determine partition (hash): same key → same partition → ordering guaranteed per key. Choose keys for ordering needs (user_id) not convenience.
Idempotent producers + transactions: exactly-once within Kafka. End-to-end needs sink cooperation — the broker does its part; your sink must do its.

example.code:
Order events topic, 12 partitions, key=user_id:
  All events for user X land in partition 7 (hash) — ordered per user.
  Consumer group 'billing' (3 consumers): partitions split 4/4/4.
  Add 4th consumer → rebalance → 3/3/3/3.
  Replay: new group 'audit' reads from beginning — history intact.
example.walkthrough: Think in partitions: they set your parallelism ceiling, your ordering guarantees, and your replay units. Design the partition count for 2x expected scale.

pitfalls: One partition for 'simplicity' — parallelism of 1; the topic cannot scale.
No key (round-robin) when ordering matters — per-key order requires keys.
Assuming consumed = deleted — retention is independent; plan disk accordingly.
lessons.try_it: For a topic you know: how many partitions, what key, what retention? Justify each choice.

lessons.title: Stream Processing Patterns
concepts: Windows: tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping), sliding (fixed, overlapping), session (gap-based). The window defines 'what counts together' — choose by the question, not habit.
Joins in streams: stream-stream (both moving — needs watermarks + state TTL), stream-table (enrichment — the common case), table-table (changelog semantics). Each has different state costs.
State management: keyed state (per-key memory), checkpoints (fault tolerance), TTL (bounded growth). Unbounded state is a slow OOM — TTL everything.
The single most common pattern: filter → enrich (stream-table join) → window-aggregate → sink. Master this pipeline shape and you cover 70% of streaming work.
Testing streams: replay historical data through the job (deterministic), inject late/out-of-order events (robustness), chaos-kill task managers (recovery). Streams need adversarial testing.

example.code:
Fraud detection pipeline:
  transactions (stream) JOIN user_profiles (table) → enriched
  → 5-min tumbling windows per user → count, sum
  → filter: count > 10 AND sum > $5000 → alert topic
  State: 5-min windows (bounded) + profile table (versioned).
example.walkthrough: Streaming is batch with time as a first-class citizen: windows, watermarks, and state discipline. The patterns are few; master them deeply.

pitfalls: No state TTL — state grows until the job OOMs at 3 AM.
Stream-stream join without watermarks — unbounded waiting; define lateness policy.
Testing only the happy path — late data and failures are the production reality; test them.
lessons.try_it: Sketch a streaming pipeline for a use case you know: sources, windows, joins, state bounds, sink. Mark the TTLs.

lessons.title: DAG Design That Doesn't Hurt
concepts: DAGs are dependency graphs, not scripts: tasks declare dependencies; the scheduler figures out order. If you are managing order manually, you are fighting the tool.
Idempotent tasks: each task safe to rerun (partition overwrite, upsert). Retries are then harmless — and retries WILL happen.
Granularity: one task per logical unit (extract_customers, not extract_everything). Fine enough to retry cheaply, coarse enough to read clearly. Aim: minutes per task, not hours.
Sensors vs polling: use sensors (S3KeySensor, not sleep loops) for external dependencies. Polling wastes slots; sensors are event-driven.
Backfill support: every DAG must handle historical reruns (date-parameterized, idempotent). The DAG you cannot backfill is the DAG you will regret.

example.code:
Daily pipeline DAG:
  extract (sensor: file landed) → validate → transform
    → load (partition overwrite) → quality_check → notify
  Each task idempotent, date-parameterized ({{ ds }}).
  Backfill March: one command, all tasks rerun safely.
example.walkthrough: A good DAG reads like a recipe: dependencies visible, each step rerunnable, failures isolated. Design for the 3 AM rerun, not the sunny-day run.

pitfalls: Monolithic tasks — one failure reruns everything; split by logical unit.
Non-idempotent tasks with retries — duplicates on every retry; the classic pipeline bug.
No backfill capability — 'we cannot reprocess March' is a career-limiting sentence.
lessons.try_it: Sketch a DAG for a pipeline you know. Mark each task idempotent? (Y/N) and the rerun cost of each.

lessons.title: SLAs, Alerts, and On-Call for Pipelines
concepts: SLA per DAG: 'daily revenue mart ready by 7 AM'. The SLA is a business promise — define it with stakeholders, not in isolation.
Alert on SLA risk, not just failure: warn at 50% of SLA window elapsed with the DAG still running. Failure alerts are autopsies; risk alerts are interventions.

On-call for data: runbooks per DAG (common failures + fixes), escalation path, and a 'is the data wrong or just late?' triage. Data on-call differs from service on-call — correctness questions join availability ones.
Data downtime metrics: time-to-detect (monitoring), time-to-resolve (runbooks), and data freshness SLOs. What gets measured gets fixed — instrument the pipeline like a service.
Post-mortems for data incidents: what broke, why the alert fired late (or not at all), what prevents recurrence. Blameless, documented, action-itemed.

example.code:
SLA: mart ready by 7 AM.
  5 AM: still running → risk alert (50% window elapsed)
  6 AM: task failed → page with runbook link
  Runbook: 'task X failed → check Y → rerun with Z'
  Post-mortem: root cause + 'add sensor for upstream delay'.
example.walkthrough: Pipelines are production services: SLAs, alerts, runbooks, post-mortems. The data team that adopts SRE discipline stops firefighting and starts engineering.

pitfalls: Alerts only on failure — by the time it fails, the SLA is already at risk.
No runbooks — every incident becomes original research at 3 AM.
No post-mortems — the same incident recurs quarterly, forever.
lessons.try_it: Write the SLA + risk-alert threshold + runbook skeleton for your most critical pipeline.

lessons.title: Data Contracts in Practice
concepts: A data contract is an API for data: schema, semantics, SLAs, and ownership — agreed between producer and consumer. Without it, every pipeline is built on assumptions.
The contract contents: fields + types + nullability, freshness SLA, volume expectations, breaking-change policy, owner contact. One page per dataset.
Enforce at the boundary: schema validation on ingest (Great Expectations, dbt tests), freshness monitors, volume anomaly alerts. The contract without enforcement is a wish.
Version the contract: v1 → v2 with migration notes, dual-publish during transition. Breaking changes follow the deprecation playbook, not surprises.
Start with the critical 10 datasets: contracts for everything is a multi-year program; contracts for the top 10 is a quarter. Prioritize by blast radius.

example.code:
Contract: orders.events v2
  Schema: order_id (string, not null), amount (decimal, >= 0), ...
  Freshness: < 15 min lag (alert at 30)
  Volume: 1M-5M/day (alert outside band)
  Breaking changes: 30-day notice, v3 dual-published
  Owner: checkout-team #data-contracts
example.walkthrough: Data contracts turn tribal knowledge into enforceable agreements. Start with 10; the pattern sells itself after the first prevented incident.

pitfalls: Contracts for everything day one — boil the ocean; start with the critical 10.
No enforcement — a contract nobody checks is documentation theater.
Producer-only authorship — consumers must co-sign; the contract is bilateral.
lessons.try_it: Draft a one-page contract for your most critical dataset. Who co-signs? What breaks without it?

lessons.title: Lineage: Knowing Where Data Comes From
concepts: Lineage answers: where did this number come from, what transforms it, who else uses it? Column-level lineage is the gold standard; table-level is the minimum.
Automated lineage (from query logs, dbt manifests, OpenLineage) beats manual docs: it stays current because it is generated, not written. Manual lineage rots.
Impact analysis is lineage in reverse: 'if I change this column, what breaks?' Before any migration, run the impact query — the downstream list is your test plan.
Root-cause analysis is lineage forward: 'the dashboard is wrong' → trace back through transforms to the source. Lineage turns a day of hunting into an hour of tracing.
Make lineage visible: embed it in the BI tool, the data catalog, the incident channel. Lineage in a wiki nobody opens is lineage wasted.

example.code:
Incident: 'revenue dashboard dropped 20%'.
  Lineage trace: dashboard → mart → transform v14 → source API
  Found: source API added a filter param default; transform not updated.
  Fix: 1-line change. Diagnosis: 20 minutes (with lineage) vs 2 days (without).
example.walkthrough: Lineage is the map of your data territory. Incidents, migrations, and audits all go faster with the map — invest in generating it automatically.

pitfalls: Manual lineage docs — outdated before the ink dries; automate from logs/manifests.
Table-level only for debugging — column-level is what you need when the number is wrong.
Lineage nobody can find — embed where the work happens (BI, incidents, PRs).
lessons.try_it: Trace one metric you own back to its source, manually, through every transform. How many hops? That is your lineage gap.

lessons.title: Slowly Changing Dimensions in Practice
concepts: SCD Type 1 overwrites (current state only — history destroyed), Type 2 versions rows with effective dates (full history preserved), Type 3 keeps 'current + previous' columns (limited history). Choose by the question the business asks: 'as-was' reporting needs Type 2.

Type 2 mechanics: surrogate key on the dimension, effective_start/effective_end dates, current_flag. The fact table stores the surrogate key valid AT TRANSACTION TIME — that's what freezes history correctly.

Serve both audiences from one dimension: finance queries the versioned rows for historically-correct reporting; sales queries a current-flag view for 'today's segment on everything.' One dimension, two lenses — no duplicate pipelines.

Mini-dimensions for fast-changing attributes: if one attribute (like a daily score) changes constantly, splitting it into its own junk/mini-dimension avoids versioning the whole customer row daily — a Type 2 explosion contained.

example.code:
-- Type 2 customer dimension
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (
  customer_sk INT, customer_id INT,
  segment VARCHAR,           -- versioned attribute
  eff_start DATE, eff_end DATE, is_current BOOLEAN
);
-- fact joins on the key valid at transaction time:
-- ... JOIN dim_customer d ON f.customer_sk = d.customer_sk
-- finance: as-was (all versions) | sales: WHERE is_current
example.walkthrough: Version the dimension with surrogate keys and effective dates; the fact table's surrogate key captures 'who the customer was then.' Finance gets restatements that survive audits, sales gets the current-flag view. When one attribute churns daily, split it into a mini-dimension instead of versioning the world.

pitfalls: Type 1 overwrite on attributes finance reports historically — restatements become impossible.
Joining facts to the dimension on natural key instead of surrogate key, collapsing all versions into one.
Versioning the entire wide dimension for one volatile attribute — the mini-dimension exists for this.
lessons.try_it: Model a customer dimension with a changing segment: write the Type 2 rows for two changes, then write the finance (as-was) and sales (current) queries against it.

lessons.title: Idempotent Loads by Design
concepts: Idempotency means re-running a load produces the same result as running it once. It's the property that makes retries safe — and retries WILL happen (failures, deploys, backfills).

The patterns: partition-overwrite (delete the target partition, then write — rerun = same state), staging-swap (load into staging, atomically swap into production — readers never see partial state), and merge-on-key (upsert keyed on the natural/primary key — redelivery collapses).
Staging-swap additionally solves the reader problem: dashboards querying the live table never see a half-loaded partition. In-place appends expose every intermediate state to every reader.
Design idempotency FIRST, not after the first double-count incident: every new pipeline's design review asks 'what happens when this runs twice?' If the answer is 'bad things,' the design isn't done.

example.walkthrough: Compute the partition into a staging table, validate it (counts, sums, null checks) BEFORE it touches production, then swap atomically. A failed run leaves the old partition intact; a retried run reproduces the identical result. The validation step between compute and swap is where bad data gets caught instead of published.

pitfalls: In-place appends with no transaction boundary — the classic double-count on retry.
Validating AFTER publishing instead of between staging and swap.
Assuming the orchestrator's retry won't fire — retries are a when, not an if.
lessons.try_it: Take one append-based pipeline you own and redesign it as partition-overwrite with staging validation; write the 'runs twice' proof (what's the table state after two runs?).

lessons.title: Medallion Architecture That Works
concepts: Medallion layers are contracts, not folders: Bronze = faithful raw landing (append-only, with retention policy), Silver = cleaned/conformed (dedupe, schema enforcement, incremental), Gold = business-ready aggregates (one per use case, owned).

Bronze needs a retention and partitioning policy or it becomes a swamp: partition by event date, retain per compliance need (not 'forever just in case'), and prune unused columns at landing — 'just in case' payloads are the hidden cost driver.

Silver reads incrementally from bronze's latest partitions — full reprocessing daily is what drowns silver jobs. Watermarks or partition-cursors make silver's work proportional to new data, not total data.

Gold is product thinking: each gold table serves a named consumer (the exec dashboard, the ML feature set) with an SLA. Unowned gold tables rot; assign every gold table an owner and a freshness contract.

example.code:
-- layer contracts:
-- bronze.events: PARTITIONED BY (dt), RETAIN 90 DAYS, append-only raw
-- silver.orders: incremental from bronze where dt > watermark,
--                deduped on order_id, schema-enforced
-- gold.daily_revenue: rebuilt daily by 7 AM, owner: finance-analytics,
--                SLA: available by 8 AM, reconciled to silver counts
example.walkthrough: Write the contract for each layer before building: bronze's retention and partitioning, silver's incremental cursor and dedup key, gold's consumer, owner, and SLA. The contracts turn 'the pipeline is slow' into 'silver breached its 7 AM contract' — diagnosable, ownable, fixable.

pitfalls: Bronze without retention — the swamp that drowns everything downstream.
Silver full-refreshing daily over ever-growing bronze — the drowning pattern.
Gold tables with no owner or SLA — they rot silently until someone important queries them.
lessons.try_it: Write the three layer contracts for one of your pipelines; identify which contract is currently violated (retention? incremental? ownership?).

lessons.title: Event Time vs Processing Time
concepts: Processing time is your server's clock: it measures when YOU saw the event. Event time is the event's own timestamp: it measures when the thing HAPPENED. Outages, retries, and backfills corrupt processing time; event time survives all of them.

Watermarks make event time practical: a watermark of '10 minutes' declares 'we believe we've seen everything up to T-10min,' letting windows close and emit. It's a latency/correctness trade-off knob, not a data-deletion policy.

Late data needs a policy, not a shrug: keep the watermark tight for the real-time view, and run a batch reconciliation tier that recomputes from the raw log including late events. Streaming for speed, batch for truth.
Session windows (grouping by activity gaps) are the event-time-native way to do sessions — processing-time sessionization breaks the moment events arrive out of order, which is always.

example.code:
-- event-time hourly revenue, 10-min watermark
SELECT window_start, SUM(amount)
FROM orders_stream
-- event time: order_placed_at, NOT arrival time
GROUP BY TUMBLE(order_placed_at, INTERVAL '1 hour')
-- watermark: EMIT when watermark passes window end + 10 min
-- late events (>10 min): routed to side output for batch reconciliation
example.walkthrough: Window on the order's own timestamp so a 2-hour outage's recovered events land in their correct historical hours. The 10-minute watermark bounds how long windows wait — dashboards stay fresh. Late events go to a side output that the daily batch reconciliation folds back in, so finance's numbers converge to truth.

pitfalls: Windowing on processing time — every outage permanently misattributes hours.
Setting the watermark to hours 'to be safe' — making every dashboard hours stale.
Silently dropping late events — finance's numbers never reconcile and trust erodes.
lessons.try_it: Take a streaming aggregation you own: identify which timestamp it windows on, and simulate a 1-hour outage — where do the recovered events land?

lessons.title: Designing Idempotent DAGs
concepts: Every task must be safely re-runnable: the orchestrator WILL retry tasks (failures, timeouts, manual reruns, backfills). A task that double-counts on retry is a bug waiting for 3 AM.

Idempotency patterns per task type: extract = checkpoint cursors (resume, don't restart); transform = partition-overwrite writes; load = merge-on-key or staging-swap. The pattern follows the task's position in the pipeline.

Failure semantics need design: trigger rules so downstream tasks SKIP (not fail) when upstream fails — one failure, not forty. Alert routing fires on the FIRST failed task; everything downstream is echo.
Backfills are a first-class operation: the DAG should support date-range reruns into isolated outputs with validation before swap. 'Just rerun it' on live tables is how dashboards show double counts.

example.code:
# DAG design checklist:
# task = f(partition_date)  -- every task scoped to its partition
# writes: partition-overwrite (rerun = same state)
# trigger_rule: downstream skips on upstream failure (no cascade)
# alerts: only root failure pages; SLA miss != failure
# backfill: --start/--end into staging, validate, swap
example.walkthrough: Scope every task to its partition date so reruns are surgical. Make writes partition-overwrite so retries are no-ops. Set trigger rules that skip downstream on upstream failure — collapsing forty failures into one meaningful state. Route alerts to the root failure only. The backfill path (staging, validate, swap) gets designed now, not during the incident.

pitfalls: Append-writes in tasks — every retry double-counts.
Default trigger rules turning one upstream failure into forty downstream 'failures' and two hundred alerts.
No backfill procedure — the first historical fix becomes a cowboy operation on live tables.
lessons.try_it: Audit one DAG: for each task, answer 'what happens on retry?' and 'what happens to downstream on failure?' Fix the first non-idempotent task you find.

lessons.title: Data Contracts That Hold
concepts: A data contract is a producer/consumer agreement on the depended-upon fields: name, type, nullability, semantic meaning, and change policy. Scope it minimally — only the fields downstream actually uses — or producers will reject it as bureaucracy.

Enforcement layers: CI validation on the producer side (contract check runs on their events before merge — fast feedback in their context), quarantine on the consumer side (contract violations halt the feed with an alert, never silent coercion), and a weekly violation report to both leads.
The cardinal rule: schema mismatches FAIL LOUDLY, never coerce silently. A string→int change that gets silently cast produces days of garbage; a loud failure produces a 10-minute fix.

Change policy needs an escape hatch: 2 weeks notice OR a versioned parallel field. Producers accept contracts when agility is preserved; the versioned-field option lets them ship while consumers migrate.

example.walkthrough: Write the contract for only the fields you depend on — small enough to accept, complete enough to protect. Wire validation into the producer's CI so violations fail fast in their world. On your side, quarantine violations with alerts instead of coercing them. The versioned-field escape hatch keeps producers agile while giving you migration time.

pitfalls: Contracting every field — the producer ignores the 200-line document.
Silent coercion on mismatch — the 3-days-of-garbage pattern.
No escape hatch — producers route around contracts they can't live with.
lessons.try_it: Draft a minimal contract for one producer feed you depend on: the fields, the change policy, and where each enforcement layer lives.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Streaming Topology
concepts: A streaming topology is a living assembly: sources → log (Kafka) → stream processor (Flink) → sinks. Data flows continuously; the system's health is measured in rates (input/sec, output/sec, lag growth), not statuses.

Backpressure is the topology's self-defense: when a downstream operator can't keep up, pressure propagates upstream, slowing sources rather than dropping data. A topology WITHOUT backpressure (unbounded queues) is the one that OOMs at 3 AM.

The bottleneck operator reveals itself in rate differentials: input rate sustained above output rate at one operator while others are balanced. Fix by scaling THAT operator (or repartitioning its hot key) — scaling the whole topology wastes money on healthy operators.
Lag has two meanings: absolute lag (how far behind — normal during catch-up) and lag GROWTH RATE (positive = drowning, negative = recovering). Alert on the growth rate, not the absolute value.

example.code:
Topology trace (rates per operator):
  kafka source:      in 100K/s | out 100K/s  (balanced)
  keyBy(customer):   in 100K/s | out 100K/s  (balanced)
  session-window:    in 100K/s | out  40K/s  (BOTTLENECK)
  warehouse sink:    in  40K/s | out  40K/s  (starved)
  consumer lag: +60K/s sustained -> drowning, not catching up
example.walkthrough: Read the topology as rates, not green lights: walk each operator's input vs output. The session-window operator takes 100K/s but emits 40K/s — that's the bottleneck (check for hot keys in the session state). Lag growing at +60K/s sustained means under-provisioned, not broken. Scale or repartition the bottleneck operator; leave the healthy ones alone.

pitfalls: Restarting the job for lag — resets the symptom, teaches nothing, and the lag returns.
Alerting on absolute lag — pages during every normal catch-up.
Scaling the whole topology for one bottleneck operator's hot key.
lessons.try_it: Draw your topology with per-operator in/out rates from the last incident; identify the bottleneck operator and state whether lag was growing or shrinking.

lessons.title: Telling Pipeline War Stories
concepts: Structure as STAR with a systems trace: Situation (30s — the symptom and stakes), Task (your ownership), Action as hypothesis→evidence→conclusion at each step, Result quantified. The debugging PATH is what's being evaluated, not the bug.

Lead with the misleading symptom: 'the dashboard showed zeros, but the pipeline was green' — then walk the trace that localized it. Interviewers lean in when the symptom misdirects and the trace corrects.
Quantify everything: '2%/week silent drop,' '4-hour recovery,' 'lag growing 60K/s.' Numbers make the story real and let the interviewer calibrate the stakes.
End with the structural lesson: 'now every pipeline has stage-count reconciliation.' The system your mistake built is the senior signal — it proves the failure compounded into judgment.

example.code:
War story spine (3 minutes):
  S: 'Revenue drifted down 2%/week; pipeline green, no errors.'
  T: 'I owned the ingestion path.'
  A: 'Stage counts -> losing rows at validation -> deploy log ->
      mobile shipped schema v14 -> renamed field -> rule dropped rows.
      Evidence at each step, not guesses.'
  R: 'Fixed + contract + CI validation. Zero silent drops since.'
  Lesson: 'Silent failures need reconciliation, not just error alerts.'
example.walkthrough: Open with the paradox (green pipeline, shrinking data) to hook attention. Walk the trace step by step, naming the evidence that moved you forward at each stage — this is the interviewer watching you think. Close with numbers (recovery time, prevention record) and the structural lesson. Then stop and invite questions; the depth comes out in the follow-ups.

pitfalls: Rambling chronology — 6 minutes of background before the first decision.
Skipping the evidence chain ('then I realized...') — realizations without evidence read as luck.
Ending at recovery without the structural lesson — the story stays an anecdote instead of becoming judgment.
lessons.try_it: Write your best war story on the 3-minute spine above; practice it aloud and cut everything that isn't symptom, evidence, or lesson.

lessons.title: System Design for Data Pipelines
concepts: Open by restating requirements as tiers: latency (seconds? minutes? daily?), volume, correctness bar, and consumers. The design follows from these — a sub-minute alert path and a daily dashboard are different systems sharing a source, not one system.

Trace one event end to end: edge collection → durable log → processing → serving. The trace proves you think in data flow, not box diagrams. Name the trade-off at each choice (log vs queue, stream vs batch, exactly-once vs idempotent).

Address the unglamorous parts interviewers probe: backpressure, schema evolution, late data, reprocessing, monitoring, and cost. Candidates who volunteer these score senior; candidates who wait to be asked don't.
Close with 'what I'd cut under time pressure' and the scaling story: what breaks first at 10x, and what's the plan. Prioritization under constraints is the job.

example.code:
Design spine:
  1. Requirements: 100K ev/s; alerts <60s; dashboard daily; ML features daily
  2. Trace: SDK -> Kafka (durable log) -> Flink (alerts, 1-min windows)
       -> raw landing (S3) -> Spark batch (dashboard, features)
  3. Trade-offs: log not queue (replay); idempotent MERGE not x-act
       (sink supports it); watermark 5 min + batch reconciliation
  4. 10x story: partition the hot key first; Flink state TTL next
example.walkthrough: State the latency tiers first — they drive every downstream choice. Trace one event through both paths (fast and correct), justifying each component with the trade-off you accepted. Volunteer backpressure, evolution, and reprocessing before being asked. End with the 10x story: naming what breaks first proves you've operated systems, not just drawn them.

pitfalls: Tool recitation without requirements — 'I'd use Kafka, Flink, Spark' answers nothing.
One pipeline for two latency tiers — over-engineering the slow path or under-guaranteeing the fast one.
No reprocessing story — 'what happens when the logic changes?' must have an answer.
lessons.try_it: Design a 100K ev/s clickstream pipeline on paper in 20 minutes using the spine; then list what breaks first at 10x volume.

lessons.title: Partitioning and Shuffle
concepts: Shuffle is Spark's most expensive operation: it moves data across the network, sorts it, and spills to disk. Every shuffle's cost is roughly proportional to the bytes moved — so the first question in any Spark performance review is 'how many shuffles, and how big?'

Partitioning controls parallelism AND data placement: too few partitions starve cores; too many drown the scheduler in task overhead. The heuristic: 2–3x the number of cores for shuffle partitions, and partition sizes in the 100MB–1GB range.

Skew defeats partitioning: when a few keys hold most rows, their tasks run for hours while others finish in seconds. Diagnose from the task-duration distribution (a few marathon tasks = skew), fix with salting (break hot keys apart) or hot-key isolation.
Co-partitioning avoids shuffles: if two large tables are already partitioned by the join key (bucketed), the join needs no shuffle at all. Design-time partitioning beats runtime repartitioning.

example.code:
-- count the shuffles first
-- 5 groupBys on different keys over 500GB = 5 x 500GB shuffled
-- fix: align keys, combine aggregations
spark.conf.set('spark.sql.shuffle.partitions', 600)  -- ~2-3x cores
-- skew fix: salt the hot key
WITH salted AS (
  SELECT *, CONCAT(key, '-', CAST(FLOOR(RAND()*10) AS STRING)) AS skey
  FROM events WHERE key IN (hot_keys)
) -- join on skey, then aggregate the salt away
example.walkthrough: Count shuffles in the plan before touching configs — each one moves the full dataset. Set shuffle partitions to 2–3x cores as a starting point. When task durations show skew (marathons among sprinters), salt the hot keys: split them across 10 salted variants, join, then roll the salt back up. Verify in the UI that task durations evened out.

pitfalls: Tuning memory/cores before counting shuffles — configs can't fix a 2.5TB shuffle.
More partitions as a skew fix — subdivides small keys, leaves hot keys together.
Caching a skewed dataset — caches the skew too, then OOMs on the hot partition.
lessons.try_it: Find the shuffle count in one of your jobs' plans; identify whether any stage's task durations show skew, and estimate the bytes shuffled per stage.

lessons.title: UDF vs Native Functions
concepts: Row-based Python UDFs pay two taxes: JVM↔Python serialization per row, and the death of whole-stage codegen (the JIT-compiled fast path). At 1TB, that's routinely a 10x slowdown vs native functions.
The rule is native-first: Spark's function library covers parsing, dates, strings, arrays, JSON, and math. If native functions express it, the UDF is pure cost with zero benefit.
When UDFs are truly needed (complex parsing, ML inference), prefer Pandas UDFs (Arrow-vectorized — batches cross the boundary, not rows), which close most of the performance gap.
Scala UDFs avoid the serialization tax but still block some Catalyst optimizations. The hierarchy: native > Pandas UDF > Scala UDF > row Python UDF. Choose the highest you can.

example.walkthrough: Audit your jobs for Python UDFs doing things the native library covers — timestamp parsing, string splitting, date math are the usual suspects. Rewrite with native functions and measure; the 10x gaps are real. For logic that's genuinely inexpressible natively, convert row UDFs to Pandas UDFs and watch the serialization tax collapse.

pitfalls: 'Python is more expressive' as a blanket policy — expressiveness costs 10x at scale.
UDFs inside hot loops or per-row over billions of rows — the worst placement for the highest tax.
Forgetting that UDFs also block predicate pushdown and other Catalyst optimizations, not just codegen.
lessons.try_it: List every UDF in one job; for each, check whether native functions express it. Rewrite one and compare runtimes.

lessons.title: Exactly-Once: Delivery vs Effects
concepts: Exactly-once DELIVERY across a distributed system with a non-transactional participant is impossible — the guarantee is only as strong as its weakest link. Chasing it across system boundaries wastes effort that can't succeed.

Design for effectively-once EFFECTS instead: idempotency keys make redelivery a no-op at the point where it matters. A MERGE on primary key, a deduped email send keyed by order ID — the effect happens once even if delivery happens twice.

Choose by sink: idempotent sinks (keyed merges, upserts) make at-least-once delivery sufficient and cheap. Non-idempotent side effects (charges, emails, external API calls) are where idempotency keys earn their keep.

True transactional exactly-once (Kafka transactions + transactional sink) is real but expensive: it needs every participant transactional and adds operational complexity. Use it when the sink supports it cheaply AND duplicates are semantically dangerous — not as a default.

example.code:
-- idempotent effect: the MERGE key makes redelivery safe
MERGE INTO warehouse.orders AS t
USING staging.orders AS s ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *  -- same key, same row: no-op on redelivery
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;
-- email: idempotency key = order_id; provider dedupes sends
example.walkthrough: For the warehouse sink, at-least-once delivery plus MERGE-on-key gives effectively-once state: duplicates collapse on the key, event-time ordering resolves conflicts. For the email side effect, the idempotency key (order ID) moves the guarantee to the provider's dedupe. Neither needed distributed transactions — the guarantees hold at the effect, where they're actually enforceable.

pitfalls: Demanding exactly-once end-to-end across a non-transactional API — the guarantee is void at that link.
Paying for Kafka transactions when the sink is a keyed merge that already dedupes.
Confusing 'delivered once' with 'applied once' — redelivery with idempotent application is the practical goal.
lessons.try_it: For one pipeline, list every participant and mark transactional vs not; then state where the effectively-once guarantee actually holds.

lessons.title: Schema Evolution in Streams
concepts: Schema change is constant; breakage is a design choice. The compatibility modes: BACKWARD (new schema reads old data — additive changes), FORWARD (old schema reads new data), FULL (both). For CDC consumers, BACKWARD is usually the requirement.

Enforce compatibility in the producer's CI: a schema registry check rejects breaking changes (renames, type changes, removed fields) before they ship. The pipeline never sees the break because it never merges.
Consumers use schema resolution: read with the writer's schema, so old and new event versions coexist during rollout. The consumer handles both for a transition period, then the old version ages out.
The sink needs an explicit policy: auto-add nullable columns vs gated migration. 'Surprise MERGE failure at 3 AM' is what happens with no policy; either explicit choice beats it.

example.code:
# registry CI check (producer side)
# compatibility: BACKWARD
# v3 adds 'email_address' (nullable, default null) -> PASSES
# v4 renames 'email' -> 'contact_email'      -> REJECTED
#    (rename = break; use additive field + deprecate instead)
# consumer: resolves v2/v3 events with writer's schema
# sink policy: auto-add nullable columns, alert on all schema changes
example.walkthrough: Register every schema change through the registry's BACKWARD check in CI — additive columns pass, renames fail before merge. Consumers resolve with the writer's schema so mixed-version topics work during rollout. The sink auto-adds nullable columns and alerts (not pages) on every change, so evolution is visible but not breaking.

pitfalls: No registry — schema changes discovered via 3 AM MERGE failures.
Renaming fields instead of adding + deprecating — the most common 'compatible-looking' break.
Auto-adding columns with no alerting — silent semantic drift (the new column means something different).
lessons.try_it: Check your CDC pipeline: is there a registry? A CI compatibility check? A sink policy? Write the missing pieces as a proposal.

lessons.title: Unit Economics of Pipelines
concepts: Total platform spend is unactionable; unit economics ('the fraud pipeline costs $0.02/order, recommendations $0.15/order') turn cost into ROI input. The question each pipeline must answer: is the business value worth the unit cost?
Attribution is the foundation: tag compute by pipeline/team (resource tags, query attribution via warehouse query logs), so costs map to owners. Unattributed spend is unmanageable spend.
Frame as decision-support, not chargeback: 'is the recommendations lift worth $0.15/order?' Teams self-optimize when they see their own efficiency; they resist when they see an arbitrary bill.

Track unit cost over time, not just total: a pipeline whose unit cost rises 5%/month while volume is flat is degrading (unpruned scans, growing state, config drift). Unit-cost trends are the early warning system.

example.code:
-- attribution query (warehouse query log)
SELECT pipeline_tag,
       SUM(bytes_scanned)/1e12 AS tb_scanned,
       SUM(cost_usd) AS cost,
       SUM(cost_usd)/NULLIF(SUM(orders_processed),0) AS cost_per_order
FROM query_history
WHERE dt >= CURRENT_DATE - 30
GROUP BY pipeline_tag ORDER BY cost DESC;
example.walkthrough: Tag every pipeline's compute, then aggregate the warehouse query log by tag: TB scanned, dollars, and dollars per business unit (orders, users, events). Present the top 5 pipelines by unit cost with their business value alongside — that's the ROI conversation. Trend it monthly; a rising unit cost on flat volume is the investigation trigger.

pitfalls: Blended averages ('$155K/month total') that hide which pipeline is expensive.
Chargeback framing that turns cost transparency into a political fight.
No trending — discovering the 3x cost growth in the annual budget review.
lessons.try_it: Compute cost-per-unit for your three most expensive pipelines from query logs; write the one-sentence ROI question for each.

lessons.title: Cutting Warehouse Scan Costs
concepts: Warehouse cost is roughly bytes scanned: every full-table scan is a line item. The bill IS the architecture — 3x bills come from scan patterns, not vendor pricing.

Partition and cluster on actual filter columns: if analysts filter by event_date, the table must be partitioned by event_date — otherwise every query scans everything. Check the query log for the real filter columns, not the assumed ones.
Shared aggregate marts kill recomputation: when 12 models compute the same daily aggregate, build it ONCE and let all 12 read it. The mart pays for itself the first week.

Guardrails and attribution close the loop: kill or queue runaway queries, require partition filters on the biggest tables, and attribute cost per team so scan discipline has an owner. Visibility changes behavior.

example.code:
-- before: 30 analysts x full 50TB scans, 12x recomputed aggregates
-- after:
-- 1. events partitioned by event_date, clustered by customer_id
--    -> typical query scans 200GB, not 50TB (250x less)
-- 2. gold.daily_orders built once; 12 models read it
--    -> 11 recomputations eliminated
-- 3. per-team cost dashboard; partition-filter required on events
example.walkthrough: Pull the query log and find the real filter columns — partition for those. Build the shared daily mart that the duplicated models all read; delete the 11 redundant computations. Add the guardrails (runaway-query killer, required partition filters) and the per-team cost view. Measure the bill weekly; the first month's drop funds the whole program's credibility.

pitfalls: Partitioning on assumed columns instead of the query log's actual filters.
Building the mart but leaving the 12 redundant models running — the savings never materialize.
Vendor-switching to cut costs without fixing scan patterns — the bill follows you.
lessons.try_it: From your warehouse query log, find the top 5 queries by bytes scanned; for each, state whether partitioning, a shared mart, or a filter would cut it most.

sections.heading: Data Modeling
items: Star schema — fact table at the finest grain (one row per sale line, with measures like amount/qty) surrounded by denormalized dimensions (product with category hierarchy inline, date with month/quarter).

Facts and dimensions — conformed dimensions are shared, consistent dimensions across facts: one date dimension, one customer dimension, same keys and definitions everywhere. Degenerate dimensions (transaction numbers, order IDs with no attributes) stay as plain columns on the fac…

Slowly changing dimensions — building conformed dimensions is the core data-warehouse discipline — it's what turns marts into a warehouse. All measures must be additive at that grain; all dimensions must attach at that grain.

Fact grain — declare the grain ('one row per order line'), enforce it in the load, and build separate fact tables for different grains (orders vs lines) rather than mixing. Without the bridge you'd either duplicate fact rows (double-counting) or lose the split.

Junk dimensions — denormalized dimensions trade storage (cheap) for fewer joins (fast). Junk dimension: one table with a row per observed flag combination, referenced by a single surrogate key — 12 flags become 1 key, and combo filters become dimension lookups.
Common trap — put multiple dimension keys in one fact column.
Common trap — grain doesn't matter as long as joins work.
Common trap — finer grain is always better regardless of questions.
Common trap — add 20 flag columns to the fact table.

sections.heading: ETL/ELT
items: ETL vs ELT — ELT loads raw data first, then transforms inside the warehouse using its elastic SQL compute (dbt models, SQL transforms) — the transform scales with the platform built for it.

Change data capture — defenses: schema registry with compatibility checks (BACKWARD/FORWARD/FULL) for streams; data contracts between producers and consumers; column-level lineage to find affected pipelines; tests asserting expected schema on load.
Principle — match the pattern to where compute lives.
Common trap — ignore schema changes; pipelines adapt automatically.
Common trap — ELT means no transformation happens.
Common trap — idempotency requires exactly-once infrastructure.
Common trap — readers can handle partial data.

sections.heading: Warehouses & Lakes
items: Lakehouse — Lakehouse table formats (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi) layer ACID transactions, schema enforcement/evolution, and time travel over Parquet/ORC files on object storage — warehouse reliability at lake storage cost.
File formats — discipline: partition by common filter columns (usually date), target ~100 MB–1 GB per partition/file, compact small files (OPTIMIZE/VACUUM in lakehouse formats).

Columnar storage — parquet is columnar: values of one column are stored together — compressed (same-type data compresses well), with min/max statistics per row group enabling predicate pushdown (skip whole row groups).
Partitioning — Partitioning prunes data (skip irrelevant date partitions), but each partition is metadata + files.
Small-files problem — too fine (hourly for small data, or high-cardinality keys) → small-files problem: slow listings, metastore bloat, poor compression.
Common trap — row formats are better for aggregations.
Common trap — partitioning doesn't matter with Parquet.
Common trap — medallion means three databases.
Common trap — copy the warehouse to the app database nightly.

Lakehouse — Lakehouse time travel queries historical snapshots (TIMESTAMP/VERSION AS OF) — inspect the 9 AM state, diff against now, and either roll back (RESTORE) or surgically fix. No backup restore, no data loss window beyond the bad writes. Retention (e.g., 30 days…

items: Event — Event time = when the event occurred (the business truth); processing time = when the pipeline saw it (an accident of connectivity). Lambda: batch layer (accurate, high latency) + speed layer (approximate, low latency), merged at query time — two systems to…
Processing time — correct windows use event time; watermarks ('we've seen all events up to T, modulo lateness') let the system close windows while tolerating late data.
Watermarks — streaming buys freshness at the cost of operational complexity (state management, watermarks, exactly-once, 24/7 on-call).
Common trap — backpressure means the system is broken.
Common trap — session windows have fixed sizes.
Common trap — exactly-once means the source sends once.
Common trap — freshness requirements don't affect architecture.

sections.heading: Orchestration
items: DAGs — parameterize: one DAG template × parameters (dynamic task mapping / config-driven DAGs) instead of copy-paste.
Dependencies — a DAG declares dependencies explicitly: task B runs when task A succeeds (not when the clock says A 'should' be done).
